title: The Paradigm Shift
label: 01 — What is FSAD
text: 01 — What is FSAD The Paradigm Shift FSAD replaces the traditional handoff-heavy SDLC with a tight feedback loop where humans define what and why in markdown — and AI agents handle the how . 🎯 Spec-Driven, Not Code-Driven The specification — written in markdown — is the primary artifact. It's a living document that evolves in real-time during collaborative sessions. Code is a compilation target, not the source of truth. 🤝 Cross-Functional Pods Small teams of 2–4 (PM + UX + Engineer, or PM + 2 Engineers) sit together — physically or virtually — and co-author the spec in real-time. No handoffs. No waiting for the next sprint. 📝 Markdown as Common Language Markdown is lightweight, version-controlled, diff-friendly, and — critically — the native instruction format for AI agents. Every role can read and write it. It bridges the gap between human intent and machine execution. 🤖 Agent-Delegated Execution Once the spec is validated, teams of AI agents — running in parallel via tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI — implement the code. The human role shifts from writing code to reviewing, steering, and verifying agent output. Models forget. Hooks don't. The Hooks principle — see Claude Best Practices › Hooks

title: From Intent to Deployed Feature
label: 02 — The FSAD Workflow
text: 02 — The FSAD Workflow From Intent to Deployed Feature A five-phase loop designed for speed, clarity, and human oversight. Each phase has a clear checkpoint — you don't advance until the current phase is validated. Phase 1 Intent & Discovery PM UX → problem.md Phase 2 Live Spec Session PM UX Eng → spec.md Phase 3 Implementation Planning Eng Agent → plan.md + tasks/ Phase 4 Agent Execution Agent Agent Agent → code + tests Phase 5 Human Review & Ship Eng UX PM → deploy Phase 1 — Intent & Discovery The PM and UX designer define the problem space and user outcomes. They collaborate — often with an AI research assistant — to surface user needs, competitive landscape, and constraints. The output is a concise problem statement in markdown that frames what we're solving and for whom . No solutions yet. problem.md user-stories.md constraints.md Phase 2 — Live Spec Session The entire pod convenes in a real-time collaborative session. The PM contributes business requirements, UX contributes interaction patterns and design decisions, and the Engineer contributes technical feasibility and architecture. They co-author the spec in markdown together — design decisions are embedded inline, not deferred to a separate Figma-to-Jira handoff. This is where FSAD breaks the handoff chain. spec.md design-decisions.md AGENTS.md Phase 3 — Implementation Planning & Task Decomposition The Engineer feeds the spec to an AI agent in "plan mode" (read-only). The agent analyzes the codebase, generates an implementation plan, and decomposes work into discrete, parallelizable tasks. The human reviews the plan against the spec — catching hallucinations, missed edge cases, and architectural misalignment before any code is written. plan.md tasks/*.md test-plan.md Phase 4 — Parallel Agent Execution Multiple AI agents execute tasks simultaneously in isolated git worktrees. Each agent works against the spec as its source of truth. A Coordinator agent (or human) routes tasks, and a Verifier agent checks each output against the spec's acceptance criteria. The engineer monitors, steers, and intervenes only when agents get stuck or drift. src/** tests/** agent-logs/ Phase 5 — Human Review & Ship The full pod reviews the implementation. The Engineer checks code quality, architecture adherence, and test coverage. UX validates the interface against design decisions in the spec. The PM validates against user stories and acceptance criteria. Reviews focus on spec compliance, not syntax — because agents produce consistent code from living specs. Then ship. PR review spec-diff.md deploy Spec-driven, not code-driven. Structure is permanent; prompting is temporary. The FSAD thesis

title: Small Teams, Shared Context
label: 03 — The FSAD Pod
text: 03 — The FSAD Pod Small Teams, Shared Context The Markdown is the Meeting In FSAD, the spec.md file replaces most of the ceremony of traditional development — the Jira tickets, the Figma handoffs, the sprint planning debates, the slack threads asking "what did we decide?" PM contributes user intent, business constraints, success metrics, and acceptance criteria directly into the spec. UX Designer contributes interaction patterns, component decisions, layout descriptions, and accessibility requirements — inline, not as a separate Figma file. Engineer contributes technical constraints, data models, API contracts, and architecture decisions — and validates feasibility in real-time. AI Agents consume the spec and execute implementation in parallel — the "workforce" that the pod directs.

title: Why Markdown Changes Everything
label: 04 — The Markdown Layer
text: 04 — The Markdown Layer Why Markdown Changes Everything Markdown has evolved from passive documentation into an active instruction layer that governs AI behavior. It's the universal interface between human intent and agent execution. spec.md — The Shared Source of Truth # Feature: Notification Preferences ## User Story As a mobile user, I want per-channel notification controls so I can reduce noise without missing critical alerts. ## UX Decisions - Toggle pattern: iOS-style switches - Grouping: By channel (push, email, SMS) - Default state: All enabled on signup - Quiet hours: Time-range picker <!-- UX: reviewed with accessibility team --> ## Technical Spec - Data model: preferences JSONB column - API: PATCH /users/:id/preferences - Validation: At least 1 channel active - Performance: < 200ms p95 response AGENTS.md — Instructions for Agent Execution # Project: NotifyPro ## Architecture Monorepo. React frontend, Node API, PostgreSQL. Follow existing patterns. ## Conventions - Components: functional + hooks only - Styling: Tailwind utility classes - State: Zustand for client state - Tests: Vitest. Min 80% coverage. ## Guardrails - Never modify auth or billing modules - Run `pnpm lint && pnpm test` before committing any change - Each task = one atomic commit # Agent reads this on every session

title: Two Worlds Compared
label: 05 — FSAD vs. Traditional Agile/Scrum
text: 05 — FSAD vs. Traditional Agile/Scrum Two Worlds Compared FSAD doesn't reject Agile values — it fulfills them by removing the ceremony that slowed teams down. Traditional Agile/Scrum — Feature Delivery Sprint Planning Design Handoff Development QA Deploy Planning Design & Handoff Development QA Deploy Typical: 2–4 weeks per feature FSAD — Feature Delivery Live Spec Session (Pod) Plan Agent Execution ∥ Review & Ship Collaborative Spec (PM+UX+Eng) Agent Plan + Parallel Execution Human Review Typical: 1–3 days per feature Dimension Traditional Agile / Scrum FSAD Source of Truth Jira tickets, Confluence docs, Figma files — scattered across tools. Often outdated or conflicting. A single spec.md in the repo. Version-controlled, diff-friendly, always current. Team Structure Separate PM, design, and engineering functions. Handoffs between roles. Scrum team of 5–9. Cross-functional pod of 2–4. PM, UX, and Engineer co-author the spec in the same session. Planning Cadence Sprint planning every 2 weeks. Backlog grooming. Story point estimation. Daily standups. Continuous flow. Features specced, planned, and executed in hours to days. No sprint boundaries. Design Process UX creates mockups in Figma → handoff → engineers interpret → back-and-forth. UX writes design decisions directly into the spec. Agents consume them as instructions. Code Generation Engineers manually write all code. Speed limited by human throughput. AI agents generate code from spec in parallel. Engineers review and verify. Cycle Time 2–4 week sprints. Features may span multiple sprints. Hours to days. Spec-to-deployment loop measured in hours. Knowledge Retention Decisions live in Slack threads, meeting notes, people's heads. Every decision captured in markdown files committed to the repo. Quality Assurance Separate QA phase. Manual + automated tests written by engineers. Tests generated alongside code from spec acceptance criteria. QA is embedded. Role of Engineers Primary code authors. Value = lines of code, story points. Architects, spec authors, agent orchestrators. Value = outcomes shipped. Scalability Adding people adds communication overhead (Brooks's Law). Scaling = adding more agents, not more people. Pod of 3 directs N agents.

title: The Advantages
label: 06 — Why FSAD Wins
text: 06 — Why FSAD Wins The Advantages Cycle Time Compression Eliminating handoffs and delegating implementation to parallel agents compresses 2–4 week sprints into 1–3 days. No Handoff Latency No more Figma → Jira → Slack → Code chain. Design decisions reach code without translation loss. Parallel Execution Multiple agents in isolated worktrees implement different parts of the spec simultaneously. Single Source of Truth spec.md replaces the constellation of Jira, Confluence, Figma, Slack threads, and meeting notes. Knowledge Compound Better specs produce better agent output, which produces cleaner codebases, which produces even better agent output. A virtuous cycle. Democratized Contribution PMs and designers contribute directly to the artifact that drives implementation. No code required.

title: Strengths & Challenges
label: 07 — Honest Tradeoffs
text: 07 — Honest Tradeoffs Strengths & Challenges FSAD ✦ Strengths Radical Cycle Time Reduction Compresses spec-to-ship from weeks to days via agent parallelism. Eliminates Interpretation Drift The spec humans validate is the same artifact agents read. Scales Without Headcount A 3-person pod outputs at the rate of a 10–15 person traditional team. Built-in Institutional Knowledge Specs and decision logs live in the repo. Onboarding = reading markdown. Higher-Quality First Drafts Agent-generated code from structured specs is more consistent than code under sprint pressure. ✦ Challenges High Spec Quality Bar Garbage in, garbage out. Vague specs produce hallucinated code. Non-Deterministic Agents Agents can ignore, duplicate, or over-interpret specs. Human review is critical. Cultural Shift Required Engineers shift to orchestration; PMs and designers must learn structured markdown. Tooling Is Maturing The ecosystem evolves rapidly. Teams must stay current. Not for All Problems Novel research and deeply creative work still require human coding. Traditional Agile/Scrum ✦ Strengths Battle-Tested Decades of refinement. Clear roles, ceremonies, massive training ecosystem. Predictable Cadence Sprint rhythm gives stakeholders reliable forecasting. Human Craftsmanship Engineers deeply understand code they write. No black-box risk. No AI Dependency Works without AI tooling, model quality, or spec-writing discipline. ✦ Challenges Handoff Overhead PM → Design → Engineering chain introduces latency and lost context. Ceremony Overhead Planning, grooming, standups, retros consume hours without producing value. Brooks's Law Adding engineers adds communication overhead. Doesn't scale linearly. Knowledge Trapped in People Context leaves when team members leave.

title: FSAD is not post-Agile. It's Agile fulfilled.
label: The Bottom Line
text: The Bottom Line FSAD is not post-Agile. It's Agile fulfilled. The Agile Manifesto valued "individuals and interactions over processes and tools" and "working software over comprehensive documentation." FSAD delivers on both — by making the spec a live interaction between individuals, and by compiling that spec into working software through AI agents in hours, not weeks.

title: Choose the Right Pod for the Work
label: 01 — Pod Explorer
text: 01 — Pod Explorer Choose the Right Pod for the Work Click a configuration to explore its composition, when it works best, and the artifacts it produces. 🎯 The Triad 3 ⚡ Builder Duo 2 🎨 Experience 3 🔷 Full Stack 4 🛠 Platform 2 🔬 Discovery 3 🧪 QA Pod 2 The default FSAD pod. One Product Manager, one UX Designer, and one Engineer work as a single unit — co-authoring the spec in real-time, with no handoffs. This covers the full spectrum of product intent, user experience, and technical execution in the smallest group that can make complete decisions. Role Responsibilities 🎯 Product Manager Owns problem statement, user stories, acceptance criteria, and success metrics. Frames the "what" and "why." Validates agent output against business intent. 🎨 UX Designer Contributes interaction patterns, component choices, layout, and accessibility as structured markdown. Replaces the Figma-then-handoff pattern with inline design decisions. ⚙️ Engineer Contributes architecture, data models, API contracts, and constraints. Orchestrates agents during execution. Reviews code quality and architectural coherence. 🤖 AI Agents Consume spec.md and AGENTS.md to generate implementation in parallel via isolated git worktrees. Directed by the Engineer, constrained by the spec. When To Use User-facing features with both UI and backend work New product areas requiring full alignment Features where UX decisions impact architecture Your default pod for standard product development Key Artifacts spec.md — Full feature spec with business, UX, and technical sections AGENTS.md — Project-level agent instructions and guardrails plan.md — Agent-generated implementation plan tasks/*.md — Decomposed, parallelizable work units The leanest FSAD pod. PM and Engineer work directly together when the feature is API-centric, backend-heavy, or follows established design patterns. Maximum speed — from spec to deployment in hours. Role Responsibilities 🎯 Product Manager Defines business requirement, API expectations, success criteria, and edge cases. Also makes lightweight UX decisions for admin interfaces or existing patterns. ⚙️ Engineer Full ownership of technical spec, architecture, and agent orchestration. Co-authors spec with PM, then immediately enters plan mode and begins execution. When To Use API development, backend services, data pipelines Admin/internal tools with standard UI patterns Bug fixes and refactors with clear requirements Rapid prototypes to validate feasibility Superpower Fastest spec-to-ship of any pod configuration Minimal coordination — two people, one conversation Ideal entry point for teams new to FSAD Design-led for work where the UI is the product. UX Designer leads the spec; two engineers (frontend + backend) ensure the experience is technically achievable. PM role absorbed by UX for interaction-driven features. Role Responsibilities 🎨 UX Designer (Pod Lead) Leads the spec. Defines interaction models, animation, responsive breakpoints, component structure, and accessibility. Owns "what" and "why." ⚙️ Frontend Engineer Translates UX decisions into component architecture and state management. Orchestrates frontend agents. Reviews rendered output against spec. ⚙️ Backend Engineer Provides API contracts, data shapes, and performance guarantees. Orchestrates backend agents in parallel. When To Use Onboarding flows, wizards, multi-step journeys Data visualization dashboards Design system component development Consumer-facing experiences where polish is differentiating Key Artifacts spec.md — UX-led with detailed interaction patterns components.md — Component tree and state descriptions api-contract.md — Backend data shapes accessibility.md — WCAG checklist Maximum-size FSAD pod for large, cross-cutting features spanning multiple services, requiring deep UX work and significant business risk. Two engineers split: one leads architecture, the other owns a specialized domain (security, performance, data). Role Responsibilities 🎯 Product Manager Owns business case, cross-team dependencies, and phased acceptance criteria for incremental shipping. 🎨 UX Designer Full design authority. May produce lightweight wireframes alongside spec for large initiatives. ⚙️ Lead Engineer Owns architecture, agent orchestration strategy, and cross-service decomposition. ⚙️ Specialist Engineer Owns specialized domain — security, database migration, performance. Orchestrates own agent set in parallel. When To Use Features spanning multiple services or repositories High-stakes initiatives (payments, auth, compliance) Features requiring specialized expertise Quarterly "big bets" Watch Out For Don't default to 4 — use only when complexity demands it Two engineers must have distinct domains If the pod feels slow, it's a Triad wearing a 4th person Pure engineering pod for infrastructure, platform, and developer experience work. No PM, no designer. Two engineers co-author a technical spec. This pod handles the work that makes other pods faster — CI/CD, shared libraries, migrations, monitoring. Role Responsibilities ⚙️ Engineer 1 (Architecture) Owns system design, API contracts for internal consumers, and architectural decisions. Orchestrates agents for infrastructure-as-code and integration. ⚙️ Engineer 2 (Reliability) Focuses on monitoring, alerting, performance testing, rollback strategies, and security. Reviews for production readiness. When To Use CI/CD pipeline work and deployment automation Shared libraries, SDKs, internal tooling Database migrations and schema evolution Monitoring, observability, and security hardening Key Artifacts spec.md — Technical spec with Mermaid diagrams adr/*.md — Architecture Decision Records runbook.md — Operational runbook perf-baseline.md — Performance benchmarks Same Triad composition but in research mode. Not trying to ship — trying to find the right thing to ship . Spec is a hypothesis, agents build throwaway prototypes, output is a validated spec handed to a delivery pod. FSAD's answer to Dual Track Agile. Role Responsibilities 🎯 Product Manager Drives hypothesis. Defines customer problem, assumptions, and success criteria. Uses AI research agents for competitor analysis and customer synthesis. 🎨 UX Designer Rapidly explores interaction models. Uses agents to generate multiple UI variants for testing with users. ⚙️ Engineer Builds rapid throwaway prototypes. Validates technical feasibility. Explicitly not building production code. When To Use New product areas with high uncertainty Exploring multiple solution approaches Customer-facing prototypes for usability testing Technical spikes to validate feasibility Output hypothesis.md — Problem hypothesis with assumptions spec.md — Validated spec ready for delivery pod prototype/ — Throwaway prototype findings.md — What was learned and invalidated Specialist engineering pod that builds the testing infrastructure used by every other pod — agents for test generation and code review, skills for coverage reporting, hooks for pre-commit and post-deploy verification gates, and MCP tools for fixture management. Its output is reusable tooling, not features. Role Responsibilities ⚙️ QA Lead Owns test strategy, verification gate standards, and acceptance criteria frameworks. Reviews agent-generated test output for coverage gaps. Defines the quality contract other pods must meet. ⚙️ Test Engineer Builds custom agents, skills, hooks, and MCP tools for the team's testing stack. Maintains fixture libraries, regression suites, and test scaffolding. 🤖 QA Agents Generate unit, integration, and e2e tests; run coverage analysis; perform spec-compliance validation; surface regressions across the codebase. When To Use Establishing QA infrastructure for a new product or team Building custom test-generation agents and skills for specialized domains Creating shared hooks and verification gates for CI/CD pipelines Reducing testing tooling debt — standardizing test patterns across pods Key Artifacts test-plan.md — QA strategy, coverage targets, and acceptance gates agents/ — Custom test generation, code review, and validation agents skills/ — Coverage reporter, regression runner, fixture builder hooks/ — PreToolUse / PostToolUse verification gates

title: Matching Work to Pod Shape
label: 02 — Pod Selection Matrix
text: 02 — Pod Selection Matrix Matching Work to Pod Shape The goal is always the smallest effective pod — complexity should justify size. Work Type Recommended Pod Size Why This Shape Standard user-facing feature Triad 3 Full coverage of product, design, and engineering. API / backend service Builder Duo 2 No UI decisions. PM + Engineer. Maximum speed. Complex onboarding flow Experience Pod 3 UX-led. Interaction design is the product. Payments integration Full Stack Pod 4 High stakes, cross-service, needs specialist. CI/CD pipeline overhaul Platform Pod 2 Pure engineering. Architecture + reliability split. New product exploration Discovery Pod 3 High uncertainty. Validate before committing. Bug fix / refactor Builder Duo 2 Requirements clear. Fast turnaround. Design system component Experience Pod 3 UX owns component API and behavior. Database migration Platform Pod 2 Deep technical work. No user-facing impact. Cross-cutting auth overhaul Full Stack Pod 4 Touches every service. Needs security + UX + PM. QA / test infrastructure QA Pod 2 Build reusable agents, skills, hooks. Engineering-only scope.

title: Compositions That Don't Work
label: 03 — Pod Anti-Patterns
text: 03 — Pod Anti-Patterns Compositions That Don't Work 🚫 The Solo Hero One engineer doing everything. No second perspective means spec blind spots go unchallenged. Agents amplify mistakes at scale. 🚫 The Oversized Pod 5+ humans on a single spec. Communication overhead grows quadratically. Split into two pods with a shared API contract. 🚫 The Handoff Pod PM writes spec → throws to designer → throws to engineer. Same sequential process. If you aren't co-authoring, it's not FSAD. 🚫 The Agent-Only Pod Fully autonomous agents, no human review. Agent reliability is non-deterministic. Every pod requires human validation gates. 🚫 The Part-Time Pod Members at 20% allocation across multiple pods. FSAD's speed comes from real-time collaboration. Async stalls the spec session. 🚫 The Duplicate Pod Two engineers with identical skills. The second must own a distinct domain — otherwise use a Triad and let agents parallelize.

title: /project:initialize-context
label: 01 — Inside the Project Initialize-Context Skill
text: 01 — Inside the Project Initialize-Context Skill /project:initialize-context This is how a project's context gets built. The skill explores your actual repos, classifies what it finds against platform defaults, and writes the docs. Click each phase. Step 0 Discover Step 1–2 Explore Step 3–7 Draft Step 8–9 Write Load the hierarchy Skill reads the full context chain Pick project (or auto-detect from path) Read root CLAUDE.md → platform defaults Read pod CLAUDE.md → shared architecture Read project CLAUDE.md → current state Assess what's populated vs. template stubs The key concept: classification Everything the skill finds gets classified against what the platform already defines: conforms supplements overrides Project docs never repeat what's in the parent docs. They only document what's specific to the project — additions and deviations. Option A: deep repo exploration Claude explores your actual code Give it GitHub repo names. It launches parallel subagents that read package.json , tsconfig , component directories, state management imports, test configs, CI pipelines — and returns structured findings. What repo exploration actually reads Each repo gets its own subagent that reads: package.json / *.csproj → dependencies src/ structure → component organization grep for @Global, Autoload, redux + UI + state webpack.config / vite.config → build tooling Dockerfile / CI.yml → deployment .storybook/ → design system presence test configs → testing patterns Findings are merged across repos, deduplicated, and classified as conforms / supplements / overrides. Option B: quick dump Paste anything Confluence pages, README excerpts, architecture notes, Slack threads. Claude structures and classifies against platform defaults. What gets drafted architecture/README.md → full architecture doc design-standards/README.md → UI patterns + conventions CLAUDE.md architecture section → inline summary + diagram CLAUDE.md design standards → inline summary Product overview + tech stack → if full setup mode Architecture README includes System overview and design principles. ASCII service diagram (auto-generated from findings). Per-service docs with repo links and tech stack. Data flow descriptions. External-dependencies table. Infrastructure and deployments. Cross-cutting concerns — classified as conforms, supplements, or overrides. Relevant ADR references. Each section: Accept / Edit / Redo — same review loop as the spec skill. Write & update Writes architecture/README.md Writes design-standards/README.md Updates CLAUDE.md (targeted sections only) Preserves existing content not in scope Verifies all files after writing Incremental by design The skill detects which sections are already populated. Re-run it to update specific sections without overwriting previous work. A project's context builds up over time — each run adds to it. Like the spec skill, it's a single markdown file in .claude/commands/ . The entire project context initialization process — repo exploration, classification, drafting, writing — encoded in plain English.

title: /project:create-spec
label: 02 — Inside the Project Create-Spec Skill
text: 02 — Inside the Project Create-Spec Skill /project:create-spec A skill is just a markdown file with instructions. Here's what this one does — click each phase to see the flow. Step 0 Setup Step 1 Mode Step 2–8 Drafting Step 9 Write Regular context The skill loads your world Pick project Pick pod Read pod CLAUDE.md Follow context chain upward Read 2–3 existing specs for conventions Detect author from git config Why this matters Before a single word is drafted, Claude has the full product context: architecture, services, design standards, platform fundamentals, and examples of how this pod writes specs. The skill does the context loading — the human doesn't have to. Option A: brain dump Paste anything Meeting notes, Slack threads, Gong snippets, half-formed thoughts. Claude structures them into the spec template. You review section by section. The key insight Both paths converge on the same output — a structured spec with problem framing, competitive lens, use cases, architecture context, and acceptance criteria. The skill's job is to solicit the right inputs and load the right context . Then it hands off to Claude's plan mode for the actual writing. We built the funnel. Claude does the work. Option B: guided Step-by-step questions Claude walks through each section with targeted prompts. Probes for the right inputs: user analytics, customer feedback, competitive signals, success criteria. Guided mode sections Problem / Description → what + why inputs Competitive Lens → web search, pattern detection Use Cases → generated from context Architecture → auto-populated from CLAUDE.md Preconditions → flags, roles, regions Acceptance Criteria → 2–3 rounds of iteration Future Scope → planned / possible / out Each section: review loop Every section gets presented to you with three options: looks good edit redo The skill stays in the loop until you're satisfied. Competitive lens auto-searches the web. Architecture auto-populates from the context chain. You're directing — not writing. Write & publish Assembles full spec Writes to pod/dir/specs/feature-name.md Regenerates pod roadmap Generates next steps (open PR, refine TODOs) Then what? Open a PR. Start coding. The spec and code evolve together from here. When the feature ships, clean up the spec as a record of what was actually built. The entire skill is a single markdown file in .claude/commands/ — ~300 lines. It encodes the process in plain English. Anyone can read it, anyone can PR changes to it.

title: /add-task
label: 03 — Inside the Add-Task Skill
text: 03 — Inside the Add-Task Skill /add-task A project-specific skill that encodes this repo's task-tracking convention — sequential numbering, todo.md entries, and the task-NNN.md template. Click each phase to walk the flow. Step 1–2 Intake Step 3–4 Interview Step 5 Generate Step 6 Confirm Read the tracker Find the next task number The skill opens markdown/to do/todo.md , scans every TASK-### already taken, and increments the highest by one. Always 3 digits with leading zeros. TASK-037 → TASK-038 Capture the title One-liner, no form If the user ran /add-task <title> , that becomes the title. Otherwise the skill asks once and waits — no multi-field modal, no upfront ceremony. Append the entry first Single-line commit to the tracker - [ ] `TASK-NNN` [Title] → [task-NNN.md](task-NNN.md) Inserted before any Bug Details section, or at the end of the list. The entry lands before any details are gathered, so the task is already real. One question at a time No form-dumps on the user The skill asks in sequence, and accepts "use your best judgment" as a valid answer at any step: source summary assessment plan acceptance Write the task file Canonical template, every time # TASK-NNN — [Task Title] ## Source ## Summary ## Assessment **Location:** `[file path]` ## Plan ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] … Why a template matters Section names, em-dash in the heading, checkbox-style acceptance criteria — all the small formatting decisions that would otherwise drift across contributors. The skill encodes them once so every task file reads the same. Location hint ( **Location:** ) keeps implementation grounded in a real file path from day one. Report back Three things, every time The new task number That the entry was added to todo.md The path to the new task file What this skill really is Not a form. Not a tracker UI. Just a markdown file in .claude/skills/ that encodes one contributor's tribal knowledge — numbering scheme, filename conventions, interview order, section headings — so every future session produces identical output without anyone having to remember it. Small skill, but it's the pattern: any repeatable workflow becomes a markdown file . title: /commit-changes
label: 04 — Inside the Commit-Changes Skill
text: 04 — Inside the Commit-Changes Skill /commit-changes The counterpart to /add-task . When a batch of tasks is done, this skill writes the CHANGELOG entry, bumps the version, and commits — in the exact sequence that keeps the artifact coherent. Inputs + Step 1 Gather Step 2–4 Update Docs Step 5 Verify Step 6–8 Ship Find the shipping set Completed, but not yet in CHANGELOG The skill reads markdown/to do/todo.md for items marked [x] , then cross-references CHANGELOG.md to filter out anything already shipped. If the set is ambiguous — multiple newly-completed tasks, only some meant to go — it asks the user before writing a single line. Detect the next version Read the top of CHANGELOG ### vN — YYYY-MM-DD ↓ ### v(N+1) — <today> Explicit $ARGUMENTS (e.g., v24 ) override auto-increment. Today's date is pulled from context, never guessed. Pull per-task summaries For each shipping task, the skill opens task-NNN.md and extracts the title + 1–4 concrete, past-tense bullets. If a task file is missing or opaque, it stops and asks — rather than inventing changelog prose. CHANGELOG.md — new block Insert above the previous version ### vN — YYYY-MM-DD **[Rollup line for multi-task batches]** **[Task title] (TASK-NNN)** - [Change bullet] - [Change bullet] Sub-tasks (e.g., TASK-005a ) group under their parent. Single-task ships skip the rollup line. README.md + HTML title Two surgical edits | Current version | v(N+1) | | Date updated | YYYY-MM-DD | And the <title> tag in fsad-playbook.html — but only the live-version occurrences. Historical vN references in the playbook's own changelog section stay untouched. Sanity-check the diff Before anything is staged git status git diff --stat CHANGELOG top renders clean README version matches no stray edits Why verify before committing The playbook is shared with engineering teams. A silent typo in the changelog or a version mismatch between README and HTML title ships to every reader and erodes trust in the artifact. The skill stops on any inconsistency instead of powering through. Scoped stage — never -A Only files the skill intentionally changed git add CHANGELOG.md README.md \ fsad-playbook.html \ "markdown/to do/todo.md" \ "markdown/to do/task-NNN.md" markdown/ often contains WIP notes. Using git add -A would catch them by accident. Commit, push, report Match the project's message style vN: <rollup> (TASK-NNN, TASK-NNN) - TASK-NNN: <terse bullet> - TASK-NNN: <terse bullet> Then git push . If it's non-fast-forward, auth-fail, or hook-blocked — the skill stops and reports. No force-push, ever. Final message to the user: version shipped, tasks included, short SHA, push status. title: 5 Habits to Never Hit Your Token Limits
label: 01 — Token Management
text: 01 — Token Management 5 Habits to Never Hit Your Token Limits Every new Claude Code turn re-sends your full conversation history as input tokens. Context accumulates — so later turns grow more expensive and model accuracy starts to degrade well before you hit the limit. These habits slow that growth. 1 Compact at 50% Run /compact when your context reaches ~50% full — accuracy and consistency start degrading around the halfway mark, not at the limit. Compacting early eliminates old tool outputs, summarises decisions already made, and reduces the history re-sent on every new turn. 2 Name the Exact File Reference the specific file, not the directory. A targeted single-file read is orders of magnitude cheaper than recursive folder exploration — and gives the model only what it actually needs, not everything that happens to be nearby. ✓ src/auth/handler.ts ✗ src/auth/ 3 Order Matters After a compact, old messages cost more to carry than new ones. Re-state the file you need immediately after compacting so Claude doesn't have to re-read it from the summarised history. Name the resource first; ask the question second. 4 Plan Before You Build Ask for a plan first, review it, then ask for the implementation. A single planning round costs a fraction of a failed multi-step implementation. One focused task per session beats five interleaved ones. research → plan → implement 5 End Each Task with /compact Before switching to a new task in the same session, run /compact to summarise and discard the completed work's context. Carry-over messages from a finished task inflate the window for the next one — even if that context is no longer relevant. compact between tasks one job per context

title: Match Effort to the Task
label: 02 — Effort Calibration
text: 02 — Effort Calibration Match Effort to the Task Claude Code's effort setting controls how deeply it reasons before responding. Over-efforting simple tasks wastes tokens; under-efforting complex ones produces shallow work. low / medium Quick asks, formatting, simple refactors, and boilerplate. Use when the task requires no sustained reasoning chain. rename a variable format JSON add a comment high default on Opus Real coding, debugging, and refactoring. The right setting for most daily FSAD work — deep enough to reason about dependencies without burning tokens on simpler tasks. feature implementation bug fix refactor xhigh / max Complex architectures, hard cross-cutting bugs, and novel problems with no clear prior. Reserve for tasks where the cost of a shallow answer is high. system design security audit hard debugging Quick reference Effort commands /effort low # exploration, quick questions /effort medium # default on Sonnet; most lightweight tasks /effort high # default on Opus; standard daily FSAD work /effort xhigh # deep reasoning, slower output /effort max # maximum reasoning budget Effort persists for the session. Reset it explicitly when switching task types — e.g. drop back to /effort medium after a hard debugging session to avoid over-spending on a simple rename.

title: Set Once, Forget
label: 03 — Session Hygiene
text: 03 — Session Hygiene Set Once, Forget Things you should configure once so you never have to repeat them in a prompt. Every repetition is a token cost and a cognitive tax. Pattern 1 Write a CLAUDE.md Any behavior you find yourself re-stating each session belongs in CLAUDE.md . The model loads it at the start of every session — you never have to say it again. ## Constraints - Never add comments explaining what the code does. - Always run the build script before committing. - Use TypeScript strict mode; no `any`. - Ask before running destructive git commands. Scope it to the project: repo-level CLAUDE.md for project conventions, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for personal habits that apply everywhere. Nested CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories load on-demand when Claude works in that directory. Pattern 2 Problem First, Code Second Always describe the problem before asking for code. "Here's what's broken and why it matters" is cheaper than three rounds of rejected implementations because the model guessed wrong about the goal. ✓ explain the problem ✓ share the constraint ✗ jump straight to "write me..." Pattern 3 Right Tool for the Depth Don't use dynamic workflows ( ultracode ) for anything a single focused session can do. Spawning 20 agents to rename a variable costs 20× and delivers the same answer. Reserve multi-agent orchestration for genuinely parallelisable work. single-agent default multi-agent for parallel scope Pattern 4 Use Hooks for Repeating Checks If you always want something checked before or after a tool call (e.g. lint after every file write, confirm before destructive git commands), encode it as a hook — not a prompt instruction that silently disappears after /compact . "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [{ "matcher": "Write", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "npm run lint"}] }] } Hooks are shell commands wired to lifecycle events — they fire regardless of what's in context. Instruction files ( CLAUDE.md , .claude/rules/ ) are re-injected after /compact automatically. Conversational instructions you gave mid-session are not — they get summarised away.

title: The fsd: Skill Library
label: 01 — Skills in this Playbook
text: 01 — Skills in this Playbook The fsd: Skill Library Twelve installable skills for FSAD pods — task management, code review, and security. Each skill lives in this repo's skills/ directory as a SKILL.md file. Install once via the Claude Code plugin system; invoke anywhere with /fsd:<name> . Installation Install via the Claude Code plugin system claude plugin install https://github.com/tbeack/fsad_playbook Skills install under the fsd: namespace. Invoke any skill with /fsd:<name> . The plugin exposes all skills to the current Claude Code session via the standard plugin cascade. Workflow Management /fsd:do-task <ID> Plan or execute any task Mode-switching skill: if no task file exists it interviews you and writes the plan; if a plan exists it implements it, verifies every acceptance criterion, and marks the task complete. plan mode execute mode AC verification /fsd:add-task [title] Capture a new task Auto-detects the current project, finds the next task number, and adds a numbered entry to the todo file — then interviews you one question at a time to write the task detail file. auto-numbered one-at-a-time interview /fsd:ship-it Wrap up a finished batch Four sequential phases: README check, CHANGELOG versioning, completed-task cleanup, then commit + push + PR. Run after do-task marks one or more tasks done. version bump commit PR /fsd:next Pick the next open task and run it Reads the project's todo file, finds the first unchecked item, and hands it straight to fsd:do-task . No arguments needed. hands off to do-task /fsd:sync Pre-flight sync check Fetches from the remote and reports local branch state before you start work. Handles all four states: up-to-date, ahead, behind (auto-pulls), and diverged (warns). up-to-date ahead behind diverged /fsd:ac <ID> Verify acceptance criteria Walks every unchecked AC in a task file, inspects the codebase for evidence, and marks each passing criterion immediately. Useful for re-running ACs after implementation or in a follow-up session. progressive marks evidence-first /fsd:estimate Story point estimation Estimates work items on a Fibonacci scale (1–21) using a three-factor rubric: complexity, effort, and risk. Accepts bullet lists, numbered lists, or free prose as input. Fibonacci scale complexity + effort + risk /fsd:init Initialize a new project Creates the standard FSAD folder structure, writes template files, and initializes a local + remote git repository — all in one shot from the current directory. folder structure templates git repo /fsd:prd [feature title] Write a PRD or feature spec Four-phase gated flow: Discovery (Analyst role) → Specify (PM role) → Technical Plan → Task decomposition. Produces spec.md , plan.md , and tasks.md in the project's planning/prd/ directory. discovery interview spec.md tasks.md Review & Security /fsd:code-review-team Multi-agent code review Dispatches 7 specialist reviewers in parallel (correctness, design, performance, maintainability, testing, API contract, security), then consolidates validator-confirmed findings into a severity-ranked REVIEW-REPORT.md with a merge recommendation. 7 specialists adversarial validation REVIEW-REPORT.md /fsd:sec-review-team Multi-agent security review Picks a specialist roster based on detected stack signals (webapp, IaC, LLM-agent, container, backend, etc.) from a library of 13 specialists. Produces a severity-ranked REPORT.md with deduped root issues. 13 specialists stack-signal detection REPORT.md /fsd:sec-review-fixes Apply security fix PRs Companion to sec-review-team . Takes a REPORT.md or findings.jsonl and produces fix PRs per finding — each with a regression test. Safeguards: branch-only commits, no force-push, clean working tree required. per-finding PRs regression tests

title: Skill Definitions
label: 02 — Skill Definitions
text: 02 — Skill Definitions Skill Definitions Each card mirrors the live skill file under skills/ in the repo. Open a card to read the full skill source — click the pre block to copy it directly. Workflow Management /fsd:do-task <ID> ▼ Execute or plan a task in any of your local projects. Auto-detects the current project from the working directory, reads conventions from `~/.claude/commands/fsd/projects.yaml`, and either drafts a missing task plan (plan mode) or implements the existing one (execute mode). Always creates a task-detail file before executing — even for lightweight projects. Use when the user says "do CBP-087", "work on FSD-031", "execute task 12", or similar. Definition file --- description: Execute or plan a task in any of your local projects. Auto-detects the current project from the working directory, reads conventions from `~/.claude/commands/fsd/projects.yaml`, and either drafts a missing task plan (plan mode) or implements the existing one (execute mode). Always creates a task-detail file before executing — even for lightweight projects. Use when the user says "do CBP-087", "work on FSD-031", "execute task 12", or similar. argument-hint: `<PREFIX-NNN | NNN> [PREFIX-NNN | NNN...]` --- # fsd:do-task — multi-project task executor You help the user make progress on a single task in any registered project. The skill is **mode-switching**: - **Plan mode** — task entry exists in the todo file but no task-detail file exists yet. Draft the plan; stop. - **Execute mode** — both the entry and the task file exist. Implement the plan, verify ACs, update CHANGELOG, mark complete. A task-detail file is **always required** before executing — even for projects with `use_full_template: false`. Plan mode runs first, execute mode second. ## Step 0 — Detect the project 1. Determine the current working directory. 2. Read `~/.claude/commands/fsd/projects.yaml`. 3. Match cwd against each project's `match_paths` (expand `~`). Prefer the longest (most specific) match if multiple match. 4. If a project matches, refer to its entry as `cfg` and the resolved project root as `project_root`. Proceed. 5. If **no project matches**: - Tell the user the project is not registered. - Suggest running `/fsd:add-task` from the project to register it, or offer to register it now. - Stop. ## Step 0.5 — Multi-task dispatch Split `$ARGUMENTS` on whitespace to get a list of tokens. - If there is **only one token**: skip this step entirely. Continue to Step 1 with that single token as `$ARGUMENTS`. - If there are **two or more tokens**: 1. Tell the user: "Dispatching N tasks concurrently: TOKEN1, TOKEN2, …" 2. Write an aggregate badge to the main project root so the statusline shows all dispatched IDs immediately. Use the absolute `project_root` path resolved in Step 0 (not the literal string, not a relative path) and quote it to handle spaces: ``` echo "orange:TOKEN1+TOKEN2+…" > "{project_root}/.pmon-session-task" ``` 3. For each token, spawn one Agent using the `Agent` tool with `isolation: "worktree"` so each agent works on its own branch. Each agent's prompt must include: - The current working directory (project root). - The single task ID assigned to that agent. - The full instruction to run the complete `fsd:do-task` flow for that ID — entering plan mode if no task-detail file exists yet, or execute mode if it does. The agent must follow all steps (Step 0 through the relevant terminal step) exactly as this skill describes, operating on its one assigned ID only. - An explicit note: **do NOT write or delete `.pmon-session-task`** — badge ownership belongs to the orchestrator. - An explicit note: **do NOT edit `{project_root}/{cfg.todo_file}` yourself** — completing agents must not write the shared main-tree todo file concurrently with siblings. Instead, return `todo_marked: false` in the structured result below and let the orchestrator batch the edit after every agent has returned. - The exact structured-return contract (below) — the agent's final message must be only this structure, not free text. 4. Send **all Agent calls in a single message** so they run concurrently. 5. **Structured per-agent return.** Each agent must return exactly: ``` {id, mode, acs_passed, acs_total, files_changed[], blocked_reason?, todo_marked: false} ``` - `id`: the task ID it was assigned. - `mode`: `"plan"` or `"execute"`. - `acs_passed` / `acs_total`: AC counts (0/0 in plan mode). - `files_changed[]`: list of file paths touched. - `blocked_reason`: present only if the agent stopped short (ambiguous plan, sync conflict, refuted AC after repair attempts, etc.) — its absence is not proof of success; check `acs_passed == acs_total` for execute mode too. - `todo_marked`: always `false` — agents never mark the todo file; this field exists so the orchestrator has one consistent shape to batch off of. A free-text summary in place of this structure counts as a failed/ambiguous return — treat it as `blocked_reason: "non-structured return"` and surface it to the user rather than assuming success. 6. **Batch the todo.md edit orchestrator-side.** After all agents return, for every result with `mode: "execute"` and `blocked_reason` absent and `acs_passed == acs_total`, mark that task's entry `- [x]` in `{project_root}/{cfg.todo_file}`. Apply all such edits sequentially, one `Edit` call per entry, in the main tree (not any worktree) — never let a sub-agent perform this write, and never batch-write a single edit that touches multiple entries' surrounding context at once (keep each `Edit` scoped to its own entry so a bad match on one task can't corrupt another). Tasks that returned a `blocked_reason` or partial ACs stay unmarked. 7. After the todo.md batch, print a summary table: ``` TBS-012 plan mode task file written — changes isolated in worktree branch TBS-013 execute mode 4/4 ACs verified, CHANGELOG updated, todo.md marked — changes isolated in worktree branch TBS-014 execute mode 2/3 ACs verified, blocked: refuted AC after 2 repair attempts — todo.md NOT marked ``` Then remove the badge file and tell the user: "Each agent's changes are in an isolated worktree branch. Run `fsd:ship-it` to merge them sequentially into your working tree before committing." ``` rm -f "{project_root}/.pmon-session-task" ``` 8. **Stop here.** Do not continue to Step 1. ## Step 1 — Resolve the task identifier Read `$ARGUMENTS` and normalize to canonical form `PREFIX-NNN`: | Input | Canonical (CBP project) | |-------|-------------------------| | `CBP-087` | `CBP-087` | | `cbp-87` | `CBP-087` | | `087` | `CBP-087` | | `87` | `CBP-087` | Rules: - Prefix: `cfg.prefix` (preserve exact casing — e.g., `FSD_Train`, `KHB-Todo`). - Number: zero-pad to `cfg.number_digits` digits. - If `$ARGUMENTS` is empty, ask: `"Which [cfg.prefix] task? (e.g., [cfg.prefix]-001)"` Do not guess. Do not pick "the next open one" without being asked. ## Step 2 — Verify the task exists in the tracker Do **not** read the full todo file. Run a targeted grep to find the single line containing the canonical identifier: ```bash grep "{ID}" "{todo_file_path}" ``` Use the resolved absolute path for `{todo_file_path}` and quote it to handle spaces. - **Not found** — Tell the user the task isn't in the tracker. Suggest `/fsd:add-task [title]` to create it first. Stop. - **Already checked (`- [x]`)** — Tell the user it's already marked complete. Ask whether to re-execute (rare). Default: stop. - **Open (`- [ ]`)** — Continue. ## Step 3 — Branch on whether the task file exists Resolve the task file path using the same token substitution as `add-task`: - `{nnn}` = zero-padded number - `{prefix_lower}` = `cfg.prefix_in_filename` if set, else `cfg.prefix` lowercased - `{ID}` = canonical identifier - `{slug}` = title lowercased, non-alphanumerics → `_`, collapsed, trimmed (only needed if template uses it) ``` {project_root}/{cfg.task_dir}/{rendered cfg.task_filename_template} ``` - **File missing** → go to Step 4 (Plan mode). - **File exists** → read it end-to-end. If it has no `## Plan` section or no `## Acceptance Criteria`, treat it as incomplete and ask the user to confirm before overwriting. Otherwise, go to Step 5 (Execute mode). State the mode before continuing: "Task file missing — entering plan mode." or "Task file found — entering execute mode." ## Step 4 — Plan mode: draft the workup Ask questions **one at a time** (never dump a form): 1. **Source** — Where did this task come from? (skip if not applicable) 2. **Summary** — What needs to change and why? 1–3 sentences. 3. **Assessment** — Current state? Where does the relevant code/content live? Inspect the repo before asking — don't ask things you could verify yourself. 4. **Plan** — Step-by-step implementation. File paths and line numbers where possible. Group into phases if non-trivial. 5. **Acceptance Criteria** — `- [ ]` checkboxes. Falsifiable ("button renders at 44px touch target on mobile"), not vague ("looks right"). If the user says "use your best judgment" or "fill it in", proceed without blocking — infer from the title and project context. Write the task file at the resolved path: ```markdown # {ID} — {title} ## Source [Where this came from — or omit this section if not applicable] ## Summary [1–3 sentences: what's changing and why] ## Assessment [Current state. Does it exist? Where? What needs to change?] **Location:** `[file path]` — [section/line reference] ## Plan 1. [Step one] 2. [Step two] ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] [Verification step 1] - [ ] [Verification step 2] ``` Then update the todo entry to link the new task file. Match the existing linked-entry style in `cfg.todo_file` (em-dash, backtick-wrapped identifier, parenthesized link). Use `Edit` with unique surrounding context. Do not rewrite the whole file. If `cfg.notes` mentions style cues (e.g. "reference task-cbp-030.md"), peek at that file first and match its tone. **Stop here.** Tell the user the plan is ready and that they can re-invoke `/fsd:do-task {ID}` to execute it. Do **not** start implementing. ## Step 5 — Execute mode: implement the plan ### 5a. Review critically before touching anything Read the task file end-to-end. Identify concerns — ambiguous steps, missing context, factual claims about the codebase that no longer hold (file paths moved, exports renamed, etc.). Raise anything unclear before starting. Do not guess. ### 5a.5. Estimate token cost After reviewing the task file, compute a rough token estimate to decide whether the plan fits in a single-agent execution pass. **Count from the task file:** - `N_steps` = numbered items in `## Plan` - `N_files` = distinct file paths mentioned anywhere (quoted paths like `` `foo/bar.ts` ``) - `N_acs` = `- [ ]` checkbox items in `## Acceptance Criteria` - `has_exploration` = `true` if any plan step contains the words "research", "explore", "investigate", "audit", or "survey" **Formula:** ``` estimated_tokens = 8000 + (N_steps × 3000) + (N_files × 2000) + (N_acs × 500) + (has_exploration ? 15000 : 0) ``` **Threshold:** `LIMIT = 130000` (65% of the 200 000-token context window) Announce the estimate: `"Token estimate: ~{estimated_tokens} ({pct}% of context limit)."` - **Below threshold** (`estimated_tokens < LIMIT`) — continue to Step 5b as normal. - **At or above threshold** (`estimated_tokens >= LIMIT`) — announce that chunking will be used, then go to Step 5a.6 instead of Step 5b. ### 5a.6. Split plan into chunks (threshold exceeded only) This step runs only when Step 5a.5 finds `estimated_tokens >= LIMIT`. The worktree is created by Step 5c — run Step 5c first (sync + `EnterWorktree`), then return here to spawn chunk agents that write their files into that worktree. **Chunk count:** ``` N_chunks = min(5, max(2, ceil(estimated_tokens / LIMIT))) ``` **Divide plan steps** into `N_chunks` roughly equal slices. Prefer natural phase or heading boundaries if the plan uses them. Each slice gets a step range, e.g. "steps 1–8" and "steps 9–15". **Spawn chunk agents sequentially** (wait for chunk N to return before starting N+1, since each chunk's output may be input to the next): For each chunk, build the agent prompt as follows: > You are implementing part of task `{ID}` in the worktree at `{worktree_path}`. All file writes must go to that path. > > **Full task file:** > ``` > {full task file contents} > ``` > > **Your scope:** Implement **ONLY steps {start}–{end}** from the `## Plan` section above. Steps before {start} are already complete; steps after {end} belong to a later chunk — do not implement them. > > **Do NOT:** verify acceptance criteria, update CHANGELOG.md, mark the task complete in the todo file, or write `.pmon-session-task`. The orchestrator handles all of that after every chunk finishes. > > Return a brief summary of the files you changed. **After all chunk agents return**, resume the main flow at **Step 5e** (verify ACs). Continue normally through 5f → 5g → 5h → 5i. ### 5b. Build a working task list Before creating any tasks, write the session badge so the task-id appears as an orange badge in the Claude Code statusline. Use the absolute `project_root` path resolved in Step 0 — not the literal string `{project_root}` and not a relative path. Quote the path to handle directory names with spaces: ```bash echo "orange:{taskId}" > "{project_root}/.pmon-session-task" ``` Then use `TaskCreate` to add one task per phase or major step in the plan. Mark each `in_progress` before starting and `completed` when done — don't batch. At step 5i (hand off), clean up the tag file using the same absolute path: ```bash rm -f "{project_root}/.pmon-session-task" ``` ### 5c. Sync and create worktree Before touching any files, ensure the branch is up to date and create an isolated worktree: 1. **Sync check** — run `git fetch origin` then `git status -uno` to determine the local branch's state relative to the remote: - **Up to date or ahead** — proceed. - **Behind** — run `git pull --ff-only`. If the pull fails (uncommitted changes, non-fast-forward), stop and ask the user to resolve before continuing. - **Diverged** — stop. Warn the user and do not create the worktree. 2. **Create worktree** — call `EnterWorktree` with `name` set to the task ID slugified (e.g., `task-tbs-024`). This creates a new branch (`worktree-task-tbs-024`) inside `.claude/worktrees/` and switches the session into it. All file writes from this point forward happen inside the worktree — not in the main working tree. Note the worktree branch name; report it in the handoff (Step 5i). ### 5d. Implement the plan steps Follow the plan's steps in order. If the plan turns out to be wrong, **stop and re-plan with the user** rather than silently deviating. Authorization stands for the scope specified, not beyond. ### 5e. Verify acceptance criteria — independent fan-out with adversarial refuter The agent that wrote the code in 5d must **not** be the one judging whether it passes. Fan every unchecked AC out to independent subagents, adversarially refute every claimed PASS, and let only this orchestrating agent edit the task file. **5e.1 — Fan out.** Collect every `- [ ]` item from `## Acceptance Criteria`. Spawn one `Agent` per AC (batch 2–3 per agent only for very long lists — never mix more than 3 into one agent, since that erodes independence). Send **all Agent calls in a single message**. Each verifier gets the AC text, the task file's Summary/Assessment/Plan sections (not the sibling ACs — avoid anchoring), and read-only codebase access. Instruct each to gather evidence and return **only** this structure as its final message: ``` {ac_id, verdict, evidence, file, line, confidence} ``` `verdict` is one of `PASS` / `FAIL` / `UNCLEAR`. `UNCLEAR` applies when the AC is unfalsifiable as written or needs runtime/browser evidence static reading can't produce — instruct the verifier to default to `UNCLEAR` rather than guess `PASS` under ambiguity. `confidence` (`high`/`medium`/`low`) reflects how directly the evidence proves the claim. **5e.2 — Adversarial refuter gate.** Every `PASS` verdict is a claim, not yet a fact. Spawn one independent refuter `Agent` per PASS claim (batch all refuter calls into a single message; a refuter must not be the same agent instance that produced the claim it's checking). Give it the claim's `evidence`/`file`/`line` and instruct it to open that location itself and try to refute the claim — `CONFIRMED` only if the evidence is direct and holds up under its own reading; **default to `REFUTED` on indirect evidence** (inferred from naming/structure rather than behavior, incomplete, or unverifiable from the cited location). A `PASS` that gets `REFUTED` downgrades to `FAIL` with the refuter's reason recorded. `FAIL` and `UNCLEAR` verdicts skip this gate — there's no claim to refute. **5e.3 — Bounded repair loop for FAIL (including refuter-downgraded).** For each AC still `FAIL` after 5e.2, attempt a repair: fix the specific gap the evidence/refuter reason identified, then re-run 5e.1–5e.2 for that AC only. Allow **up to 2 repair attempts per AC** (3 total verify passes). If it still doesn't reach a refuter-confirmed `PASS` after 2 repairs, stop looping on it — treat as a hard-stop `FAIL` and report (see 5e.5). Do not silently retry beyond 2 attempts, and do not loop on `UNCLEAR` — that's a stop-and-ask, not a repair target. **5e.4 — Orchestrator applies results.** This agent (not any subagent) makes every task-file edit — avoids concurrent-write races across parallel verifiers/refuters. For each AC, in original list order: - **Refuter-confirmed `PASS`**: edit the task file to flip `- [ ]` → `- [x]`. Use enough surrounding context in `old_string` for an unambiguous match. **Mark progressively** as each resolves, not in one batch — for ≥3 ACs resolved together at the end of a phase, replacing the entire AC block in one `Edit` is acceptable, provided each was proved individually first. - **`FAIL`** (post-repair-loop): do not flip. Record what broke and, if refuter-downgraded, the refuter's reason. - **`UNCLEAR`**: do not flip. **Stop-and-ask** — surface the AC text and why it's unfalsifiable or needs runtime evidence this flow can't produce; ask the user how to proceed (rewrite the AC, supply the missing evidence, or explicitly accept the risk with a manual verdict). Never auto-resolve `UNCLEAR` to `PASS` or `FAIL`. Never edit AC text to make a failing or unclear item pass. **5e.5 — Timestamp and stop condition.** When every AC is `[x]`, add a note immediately above the AC list using the real system date (`date +%F`, not prose substitution): ``` All criteria verified YYYY-MM-DD before commit. ``` If any AC is still `FAIL` after its repair budget is exhausted, or any AC is `UNCLEAR`, stop here and report — do not proceed to 5f. ### 5f. Optional code review All ACs have passed. Ask the user exactly once: > "All acceptance criteria passed. Would you like to run `/fsd:code-review-team` on this diff before wrapping up?" - **Yes** — Invoke the `fsd:code-review-team` skill (via `Skill` tool). Wait for it to complete. The skill writes `REVIEW-REPORT.md`; note any critical findings in the handoff message. Then continue to 5g. - **No / no response** — Skip directly to 5g. Do not run the review. Do not run the review without explicit user confirmation. ### 5g. Update CHANGELOG and version **Locate the CHANGELOG:** 1. Check `cfg.changelog_file` in the YAML (if set, resolve relative to `project_root`). Otherwise look for `CHANGELOG.md` at `project_root`. 2. If no CHANGELOG exists, **create `{project_root}/CHANGELOG.md`** using Keep-a-Changelog format with an `## [Unreleased]` header and `### Added` / `### Changed` / `### Fixed` subsections. **Detect the versioning scheme:** 1. Check `cfg.version_files` in the YAML (if set) — these are the authoritative version locations, relative to `project_root`. 2. If not set, scan `project_root` for common version carriers: `package.json` (`.version`), `plugin.json` / `plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (`.version`), `*.html` (version string in `<title>`), `README.md` (version badge or header line). 3. If a scheme is found but not configured in the YAML, show the user what you found and ask for confirmation before bumping. 4. If **no versioning is in use**, propose a scheme before writing anything. Default recommendation: **semver (`v1.0.0`)** for software; **CalVer (`YYYY.MM.DD`)** for documentation-only projects. Explain the tradeoff (semver = intent-driven, CalVer = timeline-driven) and ask the user to choose. **Write the CHANGELOG entry:** - If the task plan specifies CHANGELOG content, write it exactly as specified. - If not, propose a one-paragraph entry (placed above the most recent version block) and wait for user approval before writing. - Match the existing format in the file. For projects using integer versioning (e.g. `v36`), continue that pattern. **Bump the version:** - Only bump when the task plan explicitly calls for it. - When bumping, update every file identified by `cfg.version_files` (or the scan). Keep all sources aligned — never leave one file on the old version. - Apply the project's bump type (patch/minor/major for semver; integer increment for vNN; new date for CalVer) as specified in the plan or by the user. - If the plan does not call for a version bump, skip it and note that in the handoff message. ### 5h. Mark the task complete in the todo file > **Write directly to the main working tree.** Use the absolute path `{project_root}/{cfg.todo_file}` — not a relative path. The CWD is the worktree; a relative path would write to the worktree copy and create a merge conflict at ship time. The `[x]` mark is intentionally committed from main, not included in the worktree branch. Change the entry's `- [ ]` to `- [x]` at `{project_root}/{cfg.todo_file}`. Use `Edit` with unique surrounding context. Do not reorder lines or touch other entries. After marking the entry done, proceed to Step 5h.5. ### 5h.5. Write session summary to temp file Before handing off, write a narrative summary so the Stop hook produces a meaningful log entry instead of mechanical boilerplate. 1. Count ACs in the task file: scan `## Acceptance Criteria` for `- [x]` (verified) and `- [ ]` (remaining) lines. 2. Generate a 4–6 sentence narrative in past tense covering: what was implemented, the approach taken, which ACs were verified, any notable decisions or deviations, and which files changed. 3. Write the block to `/tmp/tb-session-summary-{TASK_ID}.txt` using the `Write` tool. The file content must be exactly: ``` {TASK_ID} — {task title} {narrative text} ACs verified: N/M ``` The Stop hook reads and deletes this file automatically when the session ends — do not delete it here. ### 5i. The steps below exist to satisfy these criteria, not just to move mechanically from prefix to written bullet. ## Step 0 — Detect the project 1. Determine the current working directory. 2. Read `~/.claude/commands/fsd/projects.yaml`. 3. Match cwd against each project's `match_paths` (expand `~`). The cwd may be a descendant of a match path. If multiple match, prefer the longest (most specific) match. 4. If a project matches, refer to its entry as `cfg` and proceed. 5. If **no** project matches: - Tell the user the project is not registered. - Show the values you'd use from the `default` block. - Ask whether to (a) proceed using the defaults this once, (b) register the project now, or (c) abort. - If (b), collect the following fields one at a time, showing the suggested default for each: - `name` — project key in the YAML (e.g. `my_project`) - `match_paths` — root path (default: current working directory) - `prefix` — task identifier prefix (e.g. `MYP`) - `number_digits` — zero-pad width (default: `3`) - `todo_file` — relative path to the todo file (default: `planning/to do/todo.md`) - `task_dir` — relative path to the task detail directory (default: `planning/to do`) - `use_full_template` — whether to create per-task detail files (default: `true`) - `version_scheme` — versioning convention: `semver`, `integer`, `calver`, or `none` (default: `semver`) - `version_files` — file(s) that carry the version string (default: `README.md`; user may specify `package.json` or others) - Write all collected fields as a new entry under `projects:` in the YAML before continuing. ## Step 1 — Compute the next number **Success criteria for this step:** the computed `ID` must be numerically correct (the highest existing number for `{prefix}` in the todo file, plus one) regardless of whether `{prefix}` itself contains a hyphen (e.g. `KHB-Todo`), and must be verified as unique in the todo file — not merely assumed — before it is ever written. Do **not** read the full todo file. Use targeted Bash commands instead: 1. **Find every existing ID** — run: ```bash grep -oE '{prefix}-[0-9]+' "{todo_file_path}" ``` Substitute the literal prefix (e.g. `CBP`, `TBS`, `KHB-Todo`, `FSD_Train`) for `{prefix}` and the resolved absolute path for `{todo_file_path}`. Quote the path to handle spaces. If the output is empty, no tasks exist yet — start at 1 and skip to step 3. 2. **Parse the numeric suffix yourself — do not pipe through `sort`.** `sort -t- -k2 -n | tail -1` assumes the number always lands in field 2 when splitting on `-`. That assumption breaks the moment the prefix itself contains a hyphen: for `KHB-Todo-0010`, splitting on `-` gives fields `KHB` / `Todo` / `0010`, so field 2 is the literal string `"Todo"` on every matched line — `sort -n` can't numerically order a constant string, and `tail -1` just returns whichever line happens to sort last (effectively grep/file order), not the actual highest number. Instead, for each line grep returned, split on the **last** `-` (not a fixed field position) to isolate the trailing digits regardless of how many hyphens the prefix contains, parse each as an integer, and take the max. This is you reasoning over the grep output directly — not another shell pipeline. 3. **Clean up empty placeholder entries** — run: ```bash grep -nE '^- \[ \] `{prefix}-[0-9]+`\s*$' "{todo_file_path}" ``` If any lines are returned, remove each with `Edit` using the exact line text as `old_string`. If the only entry removed was the last real line, treat the file as empty and start numbering from 1. 4. **Increment** the highest-seen number by 1; zero-pad to `cfg.number_digits` digits → `nnn`. 5. Build: - `ID = "{prefix}-{nnn}"` (e.g. `CBP-031`, `KHB-Todo-0010`, `FSD_Train-012`). - `prefix_lower` = `cfg.prefix_in_filename` if set, otherwise the prefix lowercased. - `slug` (only if the filename template uses it) = title lowercased, non-alphanumerics → `_`, collapsed runs of `_`, trimmed. 6. **Pre-write uniqueness check** — before `ID` is used anywhere else, derive a format-agnostic match string from `cfg.todo_entry_template` rather than assuming a backtick wrapper. The template varies per project — most backtick-wrap the ID (`` `{ID}` ``), but e.g. `KHB`'s bolds it instead (`**{ID}**`) — and a hardcoded backtick produces a false "0 hits" (spurious retry, or a silently-skipped uniqueness check) on every run for any project whose format differs. Take the substring of `cfg.todo_entry_template` from its start through the delimiter(s) that immediately close `{ID}` (e.g. `` - [ ] `{ID}` `` for a backtick template, `- [ ] **{ID}**` for a bold template), substitute `{ID}` with the literal `ID`, and grep for that exact literal string: ```bash grep -cF "{id_pattern}" "{todo_file_path}" ``` - **0 hits** — `ID` is confirmed unique; continue to Step 2. - **≥1 hit** — a collision (a concurrent `add-task` run, or a miscalculation upstream). Increment `nnn` by 1, rebuild `ID`, and re-run the check exactly once more. - **Second collision** — stop and ask the user how to proceed. Do not keep incrementing and guessing. ## Step 2 — Get the title If `$ARGUMENTS` is non-empty, use it. Otherwise ask: > What's the task title? (one-liner — I'll prompt for details next.) Before adding, check for an existing entry with a similar title using: ```bash grep -i "{keyword_from_title}" "{todo_file_path}" ``` Pick 2–3 distinctive words from the title as the keyword. If any lines are returned, surface them and ask whether to proceed, edit the existing one, or abandon. ## Step 3 — Add the bullet to the todo file Render `cfg.todo_entry_template` by substituting `{ID}`, `{title}`, `{nnn}`, `{prefix_lower}`. Insertion point — use grep to find the right location without a full-file read: - If `cfg.insert_before_section` is set → run `grep -n "{section_heading}" "{todo_file_path}"` to get the line number. Then `Read` with `offset` set to ~5 lines before that line number and `limit` of ~10 lines to get enough context for a unique `Edit` match. - Else if `cfg.insert_under_section` is set → run `grep -n "^##" "{todo_file_path}"` to find section boundaries. Read ~10 lines around the target section's end to locate the last bullet. - Else → run `grep -c "" "{todo_file_path}"` to get the total line count, then `Read` with `offset` set to the last ~10 lines to find the final bullet. Use the `Edit` tool with enough surrounding context to be unique. Don't rewrite the whole file. **Post-write uniqueness re-grep** — immediately after the `Edit` completes, re-use the same `{id_pattern}` derived in Step 1.6 (do not fall back to a hardcoded backtick here either): ```bash grep -cF "{id_pattern}" "{todo_file_path}" ``` - **Exactly 1 hit** — the write is confirmed clean; continue to Step 4. - **0 hits** — the `Edit` didn't land where expected (bad `old_string` match, wrong file, etc.). Retry the insertion once. If the retry also fails to produce exactly 1 hit, stop and ask the user. - **≥2 hits** — the ID already existed elsewhere in the file (the pre-write check in Step 1.6 missed it, or a concurrent write landed in between). Stop and ask the user how to resolve the duplicate rather than silently leaving two entries with the same ID. ## Step 4 — Gather task details Skip this step if `cfg.use_full_template` is `false`. Ask one question at a time (don't dump a form): 1. **Source** — Where did this task come from? (release note, feedback, bug report, own idea). Omit the section if not applicable. 2. **Summary** — What's changing and why? 1-3 sentences. 3. **Assessment** — Current state? Where does the relevant content live? File paths and line numbers if you have them. 4. **Plan** — Step-by-step implementation. 5. **Acceptance Criteria** — `- [ ]` checkbox list of verification steps. If the user says "use your best judgment", "fill it in", or similar, proceed without blocking — infer from the title and project context. ## Step 5 — Write the task-detail file Skip this step if `cfg.use_full_template` is `false`. Resolve the path: ``` {project_root}/{cfg.task_dir}/{rendered cfg.task_filename_template} ``` Write this content (em-dash, not hyphen, in the H1): ```markdown # {ID} — {title} ## Source [Where this came from — or omit this section if not applicable] ## Summary [1-3 sentences: what's changing and why] ## Assessment [Current state of the relevant content. Does it exist? Where? What needs to change?] **Location:** `[file path]` — [section/line reference] ## Plan [Step-by-step implementation] 1. [Step one] 2. [Step two] ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] [Verification step 1] - [ ] [Verification step 2] ``` If `cfg.notes` mentions style cues (e.g. "reference task-cbp-030.md"), peek at that file first and match its tone. ## Step 6 — Confirm completion In one short response, report: - The project that was matched (and its root path). - The new `ID`. - That the bullet was appended to `cfg.todo_file`. - The task-detail file path (if one was created). ## Conventions to honour - **Number format:** always zero-pad to `cfg.number_digits` digits. - **Filename casing:** lowercase the prefix unless `cfg.prefix_in_filename` overrides. - **Heading separator:** em-dash (`—`), not hyphen. - **Identifier casing in IDs:** preserve `cfg.prefix` exactly (e.g. `FSD_Train-012`, `KHB-Todo-0010`). - **One question at a time** when gathering details. ## Guardrails - **Always grep the todo file for the highest number first** — never guess the next number, and verify uniqueness before and after the write. - **Never duplicate titles** — scan existing entries before creating. - **Trust the file over the cfg.** If the file's existing entries clearly use a different format than `cfg.todo_entry_template`, follow the file and flag the drift to the user (the cfg may be stale). - **Don't modify other projects.** Only touch the matched project's files. - **Don't implement the task.** Only create planning artifacts; the user will do the work separately. - **Don't add a task-detail file when `cfg.use_full_template` is false.** Lightweight projects intentionally keep the bullet alone. /fsd:ship-it ▼ Wrap up a finished round of work — verify README and CHANGELOG are current, cut a version if warranted, move completed task files into the completed/ folder, then create a feature branch if needed, commit, push, and open a PR.
