title: Subprocess Sandboxing
label: 14 — Claude Power Usage
text: Subprocess Sandboxing ▼ Claude Code supports OS-level sandboxing that restricts what Bash subprocesses can read, write, and reach on the network — enforced by Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux / WSL2. Run /sandbox to enable it and choose a mode. Linux and WSL2 users must first install the required packages: sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat (Ubuntu/Debian) or sudo dnf install bubblewrap socat (Fedora). Bash tool permission checking was also improved for zsh-specific syntax in shell conditionals, reducing false permission prompts for zsh-style conditional commands (v2.1.238). As of v2.1.246, Bash permission checks always require approval for malformed commands with a dangling && or || operator, closing a gap where a syntactically-broken compound command could otherwise skip the intended approval flow. Sandbox modes Mode Behavior Auto-allow Sandboxed bash commands run automatically without approval prompts. Commands that cannot be sandboxed (e.g. need access to non-allowed network hosts) fall back to the normal permission flow. rm targeting critical paths still prompts. Regular permissions All bash commands go through the standard permission flow even when sandboxed — more control, more prompts. The sandbox still enforces the same filesystem and network boundaries. Key settings.json keys Setting key Effect sandbox.enabled Enable sandboxing ( true / false ). Equivalent to using /sandbox interactively. sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite Array of paths (absolute, ~/ , or ./ relative to project) that subprocess commands may write to outside the working directory — e.g. ["~/.kube", "/tmp/build"] . Arrays merge across config scopes. sandbox.filesystem.denyRead Block subprocess read access to specified paths — e.g. ["~/"] to prevent reading outside the project. As of v2.1.236 (macOS), wildcard denyRead rules (e.g. **/.env ) take precedence even inside an allowRead region, cover the contents of matched directories, and can't be bypassed by renaming the denied file. sandbox.filesystem.allowRead Re-allow reads within a denyRead region — e.g. ["."] to permit the current project while blocking the rest of ~/ . sandbox.filesystem.disabled Set to true to skip filesystem isolation entirely while keeping network egress control active — useful when allowedDomains is your primary security boundary but filesystem sandboxing causes compatibility issues (v2.1.216). sandbox.network.allowedDomains Allowlist of domains Bash subprocesses may reach. New domain requests trigger a permission prompt; use allowManagedDomainsOnly: true to block unapproved domains automatically. As of v2.1.191, hosts approved interactively with "Yes" during a session are remembered for the rest of that session — no re-prompting on subsequent connections to the same host. As of v2.1.243, the sandboxed Bash tool prompt no longer pre-lists the full set of allowed hosts — Claude simply attempts a request and you approve new hosts as they come up, rather than assuming an unlisted host is blocked. sandbox.network.deniedDomains Block specific domains even when an allowedDomains wildcard would otherwise permit them — useful for blocking telemetry or third-party endpoints in CI. sandbox.network.strictAllowlist Set to true to silently deny all network connections from sandboxed commands to non-allowlisted hosts — no permission prompt is shown. Stricter than the default behavior; use in high-security environments or CI where unexpected network access should fail hard rather than pause for user input (v2.1.219). sandbox.failIfUnavailable Set to true to make sandbox startup failure a hard error instead of a warning — intended for managed deployments that require sandboxing as a security gate. sandbox.bwrapPath (Linux/WSL only) Custom path to the bwrap (bubblewrap) binary — use when bubblewrap is installed in a non-standard location on managed systems or container base images. sandbox.socatPath (Linux/WSL only) Custom path to the socat binary — use when socat is installed in a non-standard location on managed systems or container base images. sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands Set to false to disable the escape hatch — Claude can no longer retry failed commands outside the sandbox. All commands must be sandboxed or listed in excludedCommands . sandbox.allowAppleEvents (macOS only) Set to true to allow sandboxed commands to send Apple Events — enables open , osascript , and browser-based auth flows that rely on Apple Events (v2.1.181) sandbox.credentials Set to false to block sandboxed commands from reading credential files (e.g. ~/.aws/credentials , ~/.ssh/id_rsa ) and secret environment variables. Recommended in high-security or shared CI environments where subprocess access to credentials must be prevented (v2.1.187). Beyond block/allow, credential files can be masked instead: mode: "mask" (Linux/WSL; macOS falls back to deny ) has sandboxed commands read a sentinel copy while the sandbox proxy substitutes the real value on egress (v2.1.221). As of v2.1.224, masking supports extract / onExtractNoMatch for structured env values, decode: "jwt" with maskClaims for JWT-aware masking, and awsPairs / sigv4 for AWS SigV4 re-signing — these require network.tlsTerminate . Hardening env vars (shared environments & CI/CD) Env Var Effect --restricted / CLAUDE_CODE_RESTRICTED=1 Full lockdown mode: removes the built-in tools that run commands or code and WebFetch (unless explicitly named in --tools ), keeps file tools confined to the working directory, refuses bypassPermissions , and ignores user, project, and local settings files. Use for untrusted or high-risk automated contexts where no code execution or arbitrary network egress should be possible (v2.1.248). CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 Enables PID namespace isolation on Linux — sandboxed commands can't see or signal processes outside their namespace CLAUDE_CODE_SCRIPT_CAPS=N Limits total script invocations per session to N — prevents runaway automation CLAUDE_CODE_HIDE_CWD=1 Hides the working directory path from the startup logo — useful in CI/CD and shared environments where paths should not be exposed DISABLE_UPDATES=1 Completely blocks all update paths including manual claude update . Stricter than DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER (which only prevents auto-updates). Use in managed/enterprise environments to pin a specific version. CLAUDE_CODE_PACKAGE_MANAGER_AUTO_UPDATE=1 On Homebrew or WinGet installations, runs the package manager upgrade in the background and prompts to restart when a new version is ready. Complement to DISABLE_UPDATES — use when you want managed automatic updates. ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_SERVICE_TIER Select Bedrock service tier: default | flex | priority . Sent as the X-Amzn-Bedrock-Service-Tier header. Use priority for provisioned-capacity deployments. ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_REGION_PREFIX Have Bedrock prefer a specific cross-region inference profile over the one derived automatically from AWS_REGION . Set to the desired region prefix (e.g. us , eu ) (v2.1.224). CLAUDE_CODE_FORCE_SYNC_OUTPUT=1 Force-enables synchronized output mode for terminals where auto-detection fails (e.g. Emacs eat ). Fixes garbled or interleaved output in unsupported terminal emulators. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ALTERNATE_SCREEN=1 Opts out of the fullscreen alternate-screen renderer — keeps the conversation in the terminal's native scrollback buffer instead. Useful in tmux, GNU screen, or CI environments where alternate-screen mode interferes with log capture. CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_PREFER_HTTPS Clone GitHub plugin sources over HTTPS instead of SSH — use in environments where a GitHub SSH key is unavailable (CI/CD containers, managed desktops, devcontainers). ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID Workload identity federation — scopes the minted auth token to a specific workspace when a federation rule covers more than one. Set in managed enterprise deployments using identity federation for authentication. CLAUDE_CODE_POWERSHELL_RESPECT_EXECUTION_POLICY=1 Opts out of the default -ExecutionPolicy Bypass flag Claude Code passes to PowerShell. Use in environments with enforced PowerShell execution policy (e.g. AllSigned or RemoteSigned) where bypass is not permitted. CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL=0 Disables the PowerShell tool entirely. The tool is now enabled by default on Windows for Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry users — use this opt-out in environments where PowerShell access is prohibited. CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP=N Maximum number of consecutive stop-hook blocks before the turn ends with a warning. Default: 8 . Raise the cap if your stop hook legitimately needs more retry cycles; set to 1 to fail fast. CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_AUTO_MODE=1 Deprecated as of v2.1.207. Auto mode is now available by default on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Foundry — no opt-in flag needed. To disable auto mode on these platforms, use disableAutoMode: true in ~/.claude/settings.json instead. (Previously required to enable auto mode on Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry for Opus 4.7/4.8 — v2.1.158.) API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT=0 Opts out of the default 5-minute idle timeout on Vertex AI and Foundry deployments (restored in v2.1.169). Stalled streams abort automatically after 5 minutes by default — set to 0 to disable the timeout for long-running batch jobs or custom streaming pipelines. CLAUDE_CLIENT_PRESENCE_FILE Desktop presence — path to a marker file that signals you're at the machine. When the file exists, Claude Code suppresses mobile push notifications. Create the file at session start and delete it when you step away (v2.1.181) CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG For unattended / CI sessions that need more than 15 retry attempts. Set to an integer (e.g. 30 ) to allow that many retries. Use this instead of CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES , which is now capped at 15 and should not be set higher. Designed for long-running automation where transient API errors should not abort a session (v2.1.186). As of v2.1.239, retries stop immediately on organization spend-limit and out-of-credits errors instead of waiting indefinitely for a reset — these are treated as unrecoverable rather than transient. CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_TOOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT Override the default 5-minute abort timeout for remote MCP tool calls that produce no response. Set to an integer number of milliseconds (e.g. 300000 for 5 min). Increase for slow or high-latency MCP servers; decrease in CI to fail fast on unresponsive tools (v2.1.187). CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BG_SHELL_PRESSURE_REAP=1 Disables automatic memory-pressure reaping of idle background shell commands. By default, Claude Code terminates idle background shells when the system is under memory pressure. Set this to preserve long-running background shells (e.g. persistent dev servers) at the cost of higher memory usage (v2.1.193). CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MOUSE_CLICKS=1 Disables mouse click, drag, and hover events in fullscreen mode while preserving mouse-wheel scroll. Set this in terminals where accidental clicks disrupt the interface — you keep scroll-only mouse interaction in fullscreen TUI sessions (v2.1.195). CLAUDE_CODE_PROCESS_WRAPPER Path to an executable that wraps every Claude Code self-spawn — agent view workers and background-service sessions run through this wrapper instead of invoking the binary directly. Use for corporate launchers, security wrappers, audit proxies, or environment injectors that must intercept all spawned subprocesses (v2.1.208). CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION Per-session cap on WebSearch tool calls. Default 200 ; set to a lower integer to prevent runaway search loops in unattended or agentic sessions (v2.1.212). CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION Hard cap removed in v2.1.224 — long-running sessions no longer refuse new agents once this budget is spent. Originally a per-session cap on subagent spawns (default 200 , resetting on /clear ) introduced in v2.1.212; concurrency ( CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS ) and nesting-depth ( CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH ) limits still apply. CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS Cap on concurrently-running subagents within a session. Default 20 ; set to a lower integer to prevent a single message from fanning out unbounded background agents (v2.1.217). CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH Maximum nesting depth for subagent spawning. Default 1 — subagents do not spawn nested subagents by default. Set to 2 or higher to re-enable hierarchical agent architectures like orchestrator → specialist → worker trees (v2.1.217). CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_AUTO_BACKGROUND_MS Threshold (ms) at which a long-running MCP tool call is automatically moved to the background so the session stays usable. Default 120000 (2 minutes). Set to 0 to disable auto-backgrounding and keep MCP calls in the foreground indefinitely (v2.1.212). CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT Holds every Claude model with a native 1M-token context window to 200K via auto-compaction, not just a fixed list of models (broadened in v2.1.223). Use when you want consistent 200K-equivalent compaction behavior regardless of which 1M-capable model is active. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_UNKNOWN_MODEL_WINDOW_ENFORCEMENT=1 As of v2.1.223, auto-compact keeps sessions on unrecognized model IDs within the assumed context window by default (a startup warning appears if this isn't holding the session to the expected size). Set this var to restore the previous behavior, letting unrecognized-model sessions grow past the assumed window unmanaged. CLAUDE_CODE_OTEL_CONTENT_MAX_LENGTH Maximum byte length of content attributes in OpenTelemetry log events. Default 61440 (60 KB). Increase for richer trace data in low-volume pipelines; decrease to cap payload size in high-throughput environments (v2.1.214). CLAUDE_CODE_TOOL_MEMORY_LIMIT Opt-in memory cgroup support for Bash tool commands on Linux — caps subprocess memory usage so a runaway build or process can't stall the session (v2.1.233). CLAUDE_CODE_WEBFETCH_CACHE_TTL_MS Configures the WebFetch tool's session-scoped URL content cache TTL, in milliseconds. Default unchanged at 900000 (15 minutes). Lower it to force more frequent re-fetches of URLs that change often; raise it for long sessions repeatedly referencing the same slow-changing pages. Distinct from the Prompt Caching & KV Cache collapsible's ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H / FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M — that mechanism caches prompt/model context on Anthropic's side, not WebFetch's local URL-content cache (v2.1.233). CLAUDE_CODE_PROJECT_DIR_NAME Optional short name for this project's per-project transcript directory under ~/.claude/projects/ . Intended for hosts that give each session its own config directory — set it to keep transcript paths short and readable instead of a long slug derived from the full working-directory path (v2.1.234). CLAUDE_CODE_GOAL_CHECKIN_MINUTES Minutes a /goal may sit blocked on background tasks before Claude checks in on them instead of waiting indefinitely. Default 30 ; set to 0 to opt out and restore indefinite waiting. Useful in unattended sessions where a stalled background task would otherwise silently park a goal forever (v2.1.234). Best practice Start with /sandbox in Auto-allow mode and a narrow allowedDomains list. Add allowWrite paths only for tools that genuinely need them (e.g. ~/.kube for kubectl). Use deniedDomains to close loopholes left by broad wildcards, and set allowUnsandboxedCommands: false in managed environments where no escape hatch is acceptable.

title: Prompt Caching & KV Cache
label: 14 — Claude Power Usage
text: Prompt Caching & KV Cache ▼ Claude maintains a key-value (KV) cache of computed attention states for the leading prefix of each conversation. When a new request shares the same prefix as a cached one, Claude skips recomputing that prefix — delivering faster responses at roughly 10% of the regular input-token cost for cached tokens. The cache is prefix-based: content must appear at the beginning of the prompt to be cacheable. The first matching request in a window incurs a small cache-write overhead; every subsequent request within the TTL window is a cheap cache read. What gets cached in a Claude Code session System prompt injected by Claude Code at session start CLAUDE.md files loaded from the project and user config Large read-only documents attached at the top of the conversation Accumulated conversation history prefix (up to the last assistant turn) TTL configuration Env Var Effect ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1 Opt into 1-hour prompt cache TTL (API key, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry). Improves hit rate for long or repeated sessions. FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1 Force 5-minute TTL regardless of other settings. promptCacheTtl (settings.json) Set the main conversation's prompt cache TTL to 1 hour (API key and cloud-provider users). Equivalent to ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H but configured in settings.json (v2.1.243). subagentPromptCacheTtl (settings.json) Set subagent prompt cache TTL independently of the main conversation — subagents default to 5 minutes even when the main session uses a 1-hour TTL (v2.1.243). experimental.cacheTtl (agent frontmatter) Set a prompt cache TTL ( "5m" or "1h" ) for one specific agent, overriding the session-wide subagentPromptCacheTtl default when that setting isn't configured. Use when only a subset of your agents benefit from a longer TTL (v2.1.248). Choosing your TTL TTL Best for 5 min (default) Short one-off sessions; acceptable when sessions rarely outlast 5 minutes; lowest storage overhead. 1 hour Long coding sessions, nightly CI pipelines, any workflow where Claude re-reads the same large codebase context repeatedly. Enable whenever a session is likely to outlast 5 minutes or runs on a schedule. Persisting your TTL setting Set the env var once in a .env file at the project root — Claude Code reads this file automatically at startup: # .env (project root — add to .gitignore) ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1 For a global default across all projects, export from your shell profile ( ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc ): export ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1 Structuring Prompts for Maximum Cache Hits Stable content first — system prompt, CLAUDE.md, and large reference docs must form a leading prefix; dynamic content (task description, user message) goes last. Multi-user / CI deployments — use --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections to strip per-user dynamic injections so the shared system-prompt prefix is cacheable across all users. Observe cache activity — OTEL events include cacheRead and cacheCreation token breakdowns under claude_code.token.usage so you can confirm cache hits in your monitoring.

title: Hooks — Automation & Guardrails
label: 15 — Hooks
text: 15 — Hooks Hooks — Automation & Guardrails Automate workflows, enforce policies, and extend Claude Code with event-driven hooks. Models forget. Hooks don't. Hooks are user-defined shell commands, HTTP endpoints, LLM prompts, or agents that execute automatically at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle. They fire deterministically — unlike instructions in CLAUDE.md that Claude may or may not follow, hooks always execute when their event triggers. Hook Lifecycle ▼ Hooks fire at specific stages of Claude Code's execution. Understanding the lifecycle helps you choose the right event for your hook. SessionStart │ ├── [Per-turn loop] │ UserPromptSubmit │ │ │ ├── [Agentic loop] │ │ PreToolUse → PermissionRequest → Tool executes │ │ │ │ │ │ │ PostToolUse / PostToolUseFailure │ │ │ │ │ SubagentStart → SubagentStop │ │ TaskCreated → TaskCompleted │ │ │ Stop / StopFailure │ ├── [Async events] │ FileChanged, CwdChanged, ConfigChange │ WorktreeCreate / WorktreeRemove │ PreCompact / PostCompact │ PreModelSwitch / PostModelSwitch │ Notification │ SessionEnd 30 Hook Events See the Cheat Sheet for the full reference table of all 30 hook events organized by category. Five Hook Types ▼ Each hook type suits different use cases. Most teams start with command hooks and add others as needs grow. Type How It Works Best For command Runs a shell command. Receives JSON on stdin, returns results via exit code + stdout. Linting, formatting, blocking unsafe commands, logging http Sends JSON POST to an endpoint. Headers support $ENV_VAR interpolation. Remote validation, audit logging, webhook integrations prompt Sends a single-turn prompt to Claude. Returns a yes/no decision as JSON. Security review of commands, content policy checks agent Spawns a subagent with tool access (Read, Grep, Glob). Full agentic evaluation. Complex verification, multi-file checks, code analysis mcp_tool Invokes an MCP tool directly. Specify the server and tool name; Claude passes the hook context as input. Calling external services, Slack/Jira notifications, custom audit systems via MCP Command hook (shell form): { "type": "command", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/lint.sh", "timeout": 30 } Command hook (exec form — no shell, no quoting needed): { "type": "command", "command": "/path/to/hook.sh", "args": ["--flag", "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"], "timeout": 30 } The args array spawns the command directly via execve — no shell is involved, so path placeholders and special characters never need quoting. Prefer exec form when your hook path or arguments contain spaces or env vars. Security note (v2.1.207): In shell-form hooks, ${user_config.*} substitutions are now rejected to prevent shell injection. If your hook needs to access a plugin configuration value, use exec form and read it via $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY> inside the hook script. HTTP hook: { "type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:8080/hooks/pre-tool-use", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer $MY_TOKEN" }, "allowedEnvVars": ["MY_TOKEN"] } Prompt hook: { "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Is this shell command safe to execute? $ARGUMENTS" } Agent hook: { "type": "agent", "prompt": "Verify this edit doesn't break any imports. $ARGUMENTS" } MCP tool hook: { "type": "mcp_tool", "server": "slack", "tool": "send_message", "input": { "channel": "#dev-audit", "text": "Tool use: $TOOL_NAME" } } Configuration ▼ Where to put hooks (by scope): Location Scope ~/.claude/settings.json All projects (local to your machine) .claude/settings.json Single project (shareable, committed to git) .claude/settings.local.json Single project (gitignored, personal) Managed policy settings Organization-wide (admin-controlled) Plugin hooks/hooks.json Active when plugin is enabled Skill/Agent YAML frontmatter Active while component runs Settings.json structure: { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "if": "Bash(rm *)", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/block-rm.sh", "timeout": 30, "statusMessage": "Checking command safety..." } ] } ] } } Matcher patterns: Pattern Evaluated As Example "*" , "" , or omitted Match all Fires on every event Letters, digits, _ , | only Exact or pipe-separated list Bash or Edit|Write Contains other characters JavaScript regex ^Notebook , mcp__.* , mcp__brave-search__.* Hyphenated identifiers (e.g. code-reviewer , mcp__brave-search ) contain - so they are treated as regex and exact-match the literal name. To match all tools from a hyphenated MCP server, append __.* : use "mcp__brave-search__.*" instead of "mcp__brave-search" (v2.1.195). Conditional if field — narrows which tool calls trigger a hook: "Bash(git *)" — only git commands "Bash(rm *)" — only rm commands "Edit(*.ts)" — only TypeScript edits "Write(*.md)" — only Markdown writes Path-scoping (v2.1.214): A single-segment pattern like "Edit(src/**)" in an if: condition matches only <cwd>/src/ — not a src/ directory nested deeper in the tree. Write "Edit(**/src/**)" to match at any depth. Note: deny / ask permission rules keep their any-depth behavior — this scoping applies only to hook if: conditions. Command-substitution false-fires fixed (v2.1.243): Earlier versions could false-fire an if condition like "Bash(cat *)" on an unrelated command if it contained $() or backtick command substitution followed by more arguments. This is fixed as of v2.1.243 — such conditions now match only the intended command. Environment variables available in hooks: Variable Description CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR Project root directory CLAUDE_ENV_FILE File path for persisting env vars (SessionStart, CwdChanged, FileChanged) CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT Plugin installation directory CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA Plugin persistent data directory CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID Current session ID — also injected into the Bash tool subprocess environment and into stdio MCP server subprocess environments (v2.1.154), enabling scripts and MCP servers to correlate tool runs with the active session without parsing hook JSON input. Stdio MCP servers also receive CLAUDECODE=1 to confirm they are running inside Claude Code. CLAUDE_EFFORT Active effort level ( low | medium | high | xhigh | max ) — injected into Bash tool subprocess commands so scripts can branch on effort without parsing hook JSON. Also available as effort.level in the JSON delivered to hook stdin. Exit Codes & Decision Control ▼ Exit codes determine whether a hook blocks execution or just logs a warning. Getting this right is critical for policy enforcement. Exit Code Behavior 0 Success — stdout parsed for JSON output. Most events: written to debug log. Exceptions: UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart show stdout as context. 2 Blocking error — blocks tool call, rejects prompt, prevents stop, or blocks compaction (depending on event). Stderr is fed back as the error message. Any other Non-blocking error — stderr shown as warning in transcript. Execution continues normally. Exit 2 Is the Only Blocking Code Exit 1 is non-blocking — it logs an error but doesn't stop anything. You must use exit 2 to enforce policy. This is the most common mistake when writing hooks. PreToolUse permission decisions — control what happens to the tool call: Decision Effect allow Skip permission prompt, execute immediately deny Block the tool call entirely ask Prompt the user to confirm defer Pause for later (non-interactive -p mode only) When multiple hooks fire, precedence is: deny > defer > ask > allow . PreCompact blocking — prevent context compaction from running: Method Effect Exit with code 2 Block compaction; stderr shown as reason Return {"decision":"block"} Block compaction via JSON decision output PostToolUse output replacement — replace the tool's output before Claude sees it: { "hookSpecificOutput": { "updatedToolOutput": "Sanitized or transformed output here" } } Return this JSON from a PostToolUse hook (exit 0) to substitute the tool result Claude receives. Works for all tools — use it to redact sensitive output, normalize formats, or inject additional context. PostToolUse continueOnBlock — soft block: feed the rejection reason back to Claude instead of ending the turn: { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/check-output.sh", "continueOnBlock": true } ] } ] } } When "continueOnBlock": true is set, a hook that exits 2 (block) feeds its rejection reason back to Claude as a tool result and the turn continues — Claude can retry or adjust. Without this option, a block ends the turn immediately. Use continueOnBlock for "soft guard" patterns where you want Claude to self-correct rather than halt. Hook terminalSequence — emit terminal escape sequences (desktop notifications, window title, bell) from any hook: { "terminalSequence": "" } Return a JSON object with a terminalSequence key from any hook (exit 0). Claude Code writes the value directly to the terminal — even when there is no controlling TTY. Common sequences: "" rings the terminal bell; "]2;Task done" sets the window title. Use this to provide ambient feedback without wrapping Claude Code in a shell script or requiring a controlling terminal. Practical Recipes ▼ Real-world hook examples you can add to .claude/settings.json . Security — block destructive commands: { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "if": "Bash(rm *)", "command": "echo 'Destructive command blocked' >&2 && exit 2" } ] } ] } } Quality — auto-lint after file edits: { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "npx eslint --fix \"$CLAUDE_FILE_PATH\" 2>/dev/null || true" } ] } ] } } Workflow — read-before-edit reminder: { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "echo 'READ-BEFORE-EDIT: Read the file first before editing.'" } ] } ] } } Policy — prompt-based security review: { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Is this shell command safe to execute? Command: $ARGUMENTS", "timeout": 30 } ] } ] } } Environment — auto-setup via SessionStart: #!/bin/bash # .claude/hooks/session-setup.sh if [ -n "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE" ]; then echo 'export NODE_ENV=production' >> "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE" echo 'export PATH="$PATH:./node_modules/.bin"' >> "$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE" fi exit 0 { "hooks": { "SessionStart": [ { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "\"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/.claude/hooks/session-setup.sh" } ] } ] } } Observability — log all MCP operations: { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "mcp__.*", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "echo \"$(date): MCP operation\" >> ~/mcp-audit.log" } ] } ] } } Hook Best Practices ▼ Keep hooks fast — especially SessionStart , which runs on every session launch Use exit 2 to enforce — exit 1 is non-blocking and won't stop anything Test with --debug — see full hook execution details in the debug log Use the if field — narrow trigger conditions to avoid unnecessary process spawns Use async: true — for fire-and-forget operations like logging Reference scripts via $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR — always quote for paths with spaces View hooks with /hooks — read-only browser showing all configured hooks by source Disable all with "disableAllHooks": true — in settings.json for troubleshooting Continuous Evals in CI ▼ Hooks and one-off checks catch known failure modes, but they don't tell you whether a change to CLAUDE.md , a skill, or a hook made the agent worse at real work. A continuous eval suite closes that gap: a small, growing library of real tasks — each captured as a prompt plus acceptance checks — that runs non-interactively in CI and gates any change to your agent-steering configuration before it merges. Most teams start with 20–50 cases pulled from actual recent work — a bug fix, a refactor, a feature slice, an edge case someone got wrong. Each case is stored as a prompt (the task phrased the way a user would ask it) plus 2–4 acceptance checks — commands or assertions that must all pass for the run to count as a success: tests pass, lint is clean, behavior outside the target area is unchanged, and any team policy (no git push --force , no editing .env , etc.) was respected. The suite runs two ways: On a schedule — nightly or via cron, to catch drift from model updates, dependency bumps, or unrelated config edits. As a merge gate — on every pull request that touches CLAUDE.md , a skill, or a hook, the same way a unit test suite gates application code. The PR can't merge until the eval suite passes. Every incident becomes a permanent test The suite's real power is compounding growth: every production incident becomes a permanent eval case. When an agent does something wrong in the wild, don't just fix the immediate issue — write the prompt and acceptance check that would have caught it, and add it to the suite. Over months this becomes a living regression test of every mistake the team has already paid for once, so the same mistake can't silently reappear after the next config change. Example eval case: id: eval-023 source: incident-2026-04-11 # promoted from a real production bug prompt: > Add input validation to the POST /api/users endpoint so a request missing the "email" field returns a 400 with a clear error message, instead of a 500. acceptance: - name: tests pass run: npm test -- users.routes.test.js - name: lint clean run: npm run lint -- src/api/users.js - name: change is scoped run: '[ "$(git diff --name-only | grep -vc "^src/api/users.js")" = "0" ]'

title: Cloud Integrations
label: 15.5 — HTTP Hooks & Managed Web Agents
text: 15.5 — HTTP Hooks & Managed Web Agents Cloud Integrations Connect Claude Code to external services via HTTP hooks, and deploy Claude as a fully managed cloud agent for long-running autonomous work — no agent loop required. HTTP Hooks — Webhook Integrations ▼ HTTP hooks ( "type": "http" ) POST Claude Code lifecycle events as JSON to any HTTP endpoint. Unlike command hooks, the receiving server doesn't need to be co-located with the developer — enabling team-wide shared audit services, remote approval gateways, and webhook-based integrations with Slack, PagerDuty, GitHub Actions, and custom dashboards. HTTP hook schema: { "type": "http", "url": "https://your-service.example.com/hooks/tool-use", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer $HOOK_TOKEN", "X-Team": "platform-eng" }, "allowedEnvVars": ["HOOK_TOKEN"], "timeout": 10 } Header values support $VAR or ${VAR} interpolation. Only env vars listed in allowedEnvVars are expanded — all others remain empty strings. Recipe 1 — Team audit log service (PostToolUse): Every tool call across your team's Claude Code sessions is POSTed to a shared logging endpoint. The body is the standard PostToolUse JSON (session_id, tool_name, tool_input, tool_output). Index this into Elasticsearch, Datadog, or any observability stack. { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash|Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "http", "url": "https://audit.internal/api/claude-events", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer $AUDIT_TOKEN" }, "allowedEnvVars": ["AUDIT_TOKEN"] } ] } ] } } Recipe 2 — Slack notification on task completion (Stop): Post a message to your team's Slack channel whenever Claude finishes a turn. The Stop event fires each time Claude stops responding — pair with a Slack incoming webhook URL for real-time task completion alerts. { "hooks": { "Stop": [ { "hooks": [ { "type": "http", "url": "$SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL", "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, "allowedEnvVars": ["SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL"] } ] } ] } } Recipe 3 — External approval gateway (PreToolUse): Before allowing destructive Bash commands in a regulated environment, POST to an approval service. Return a 2xx response with the appropriate hookSpecificOutput JSON. A 403 or 500 causes a hook error — execution continues, it does not block. Always list env vars in allowedEnvVars . Any $VAR in headers not in this list expands to an empty string — no error, just silent auth failures. Set timeout explicitly for fast gates. Default is 10 minutes. An approval gateway that hangs will block Claude for 10 minutes if you don't specify a lower timeout (e.g., "timeout": 10 seconds). Non-2xx responses cause hook errors — execution proceeds. If your server returns a 500, Claude Code logs a hook error but does not block the action. Design your server to return 2xx with a deny body, not an HTTP error code. Events Messages exchanged between your application and the agent — user turns, tool results, status updates. Fetched on demand or streamed live. Python quickstart: import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() # SDK sets managed-agents beta header automatically # 1. Create the agent once — reuse agent_id across sessions agent = client.beta.managed_agents.agents.create( model="claude-opus-4-7", system="You are a code review specialist. Analyze PRs for bugs and security issues.", tools=[{"type": "bash"}, {"type": "web_search"}, {"type": "file"}], ) # 2. Create a cloud environment with the packages you need env = client.beta.managed_agents.environments.create( packages=["python3", "git", "ripgrep"], network={"allowed_domains": ["github.com", "api.github.com"]}, ) # 3. All endpoints require the managed-agents-2026-04-01 beta header. The Anthropic Python/TypeScript SDKs set this automatically via client.beta.managed_agents . Rate limits apply at the org level. 300 requests/min for create endpoints (agents, sessions, environments), 600 requests/min for read endpoints. Fan-out architectures need explicit rate management. Novel Patterns & Real-World Use Cases ▼ Real adoption patterns from teams running HTTP hooks and Managed Web Agents in production. Hookdeck — Inbound webhook bridge via Claude Channels: Hookdeck's integration uses Claude Code's Channels feature (a specialized MCP server that emits notification events) to push inbound webhooks from GitHub, Stripe, or any external service directly into an active Claude Code session. The pattern: external service → Hookdeck → Claude Code Channel → Claude processes the event. Useful for having Claude react to production events (new PR, failed payment, deploy failure) without polling. # Claude Code Channels receive external webhooks via Hookdeck CLI hookdeck listen 3000 claude-code-channel # Claude Code picks up events streamed from the channel MCP server # and can take action — file edits, git operations, notifications Sentry — Bug to PR, fully autonomous: Sentry deployed a Managed Web Agent that takes a flagged error from their issue tracker, clones the relevant repo in a managed container, reproduces the bug, writes a fix, runs the test suite, and opens a pull request — all without human involvement. The agent uses Bash, file ops, and web search tools. Sessions run for 5–15 minutes per issue. Notion — Parallel delegated tasks: Notion runs dozens of parallel Managed Agent sessions simultaneously — one per delegated task from a user's workspace. Tasks include writing and shipping code, creating Slack channels, researching competitor sites, and generating project timelines. Session event history is persisted server-side so Notion can retrieve results asynchronously and surface them in the UI without a persistent connection. Async hooks for non-blocking background work: Async hooks (released January 2026) run in the background without blocking Claude's execution. Use them for slow operations — sending telemetry, triggering CI, updating dashboards — where you don't need the result to inform the next step. Configure with "async": true in the hook definition. { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "http", "url": "https://telemetry.internal/events", "async": true } ] } ] } } External policy engine with PermissionRequest hook: Teams in regulated environments (fintech, healthcare) route all permission prompts through a centralized policy engine via HTTP hook on the PermissionRequest event. The engine checks the tool call against compliance rules and returns an allow/deny decision — replacing the interactive dialog with deterministic policy enforcement. Because the hook fires before the user sees the dialog, the policy engine's decision is silent and auditable. Use HTTP Hooks for Team-Wide Policies, Command Hooks for Personal Automation HTTP hooks make sense when the policy, rule, or notification target is shared across multiple developers. Command hooks are better for personal automation (formatting, linting) that doesn't need a server. The two types compose — a single event can have both.

title: Track Usage, Costs & Tool Activity
label: 16 — Claude Monitoring
text: 16 — Claude Monitoring Track Usage, Costs & Tool Activity Monitor Claude Code across your organization with OpenTelemetry. Track token spend, session activity, tool usage, and developer productivity — then pipe it into the observability stack you already use. Quick Start ▼ Enable OpenTelemetry export with a handful of environment variables. Set these before running claude : # 1. Enable telemetry (required) export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 # 2. Choose exporters (both optional — configure what you need) export OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=otlp # otlp | prometheus | console | none export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp # otlp | console | none # 3. Point at your collector export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:4317 # 4. Auth header (if your collector requires it) export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS= "Authorization=Bearer your-token" # 5. Run Claude Code claude Debugging Tip Use OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=console with OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL=1000 to see metrics printed to stdout every second while you verify your setup. Available Metrics ▼ Claude Code exports 8 time-series metrics. The cost and token counters are the ones most teams start with. Metric Description Unit claude_code.cost.usage Session cost (approximation — use API console for billing) USD claude_code.token.usage Tokens used, broken down by type : input, output, cacheRead, cacheCreation tokens claude_code.session.count CLI sessions started count claude_code.active_time.total Active time (user interactions + CLI processing) seconds claude_code.lines_of_code.count Lines added or removed, broken down by model attribute (v2.1.172) count claude_code.commit.count Git commits created via Claude count claude_code.pull_request.count PRs created via Claude count claude_code.code_edit_tool.decision Tool permission accept/reject decisions count All metrics carry standard attributes: session.id , organization.id , user.account_uuid , and terminal.type . Token and cost metrics also include model . Events & Logs ▼ When OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER is configured, Claude Code emits structured events for every prompt, tool call, and API request. Events share a prompt.id so you can trace all activity back to the prompt that triggered it. Event Fires When Key Attributes claude_code.user_prompt User submits a prompt prompt_length, prompt (opt-in) claude_code.tool Tool call trace span agent_id, parent_agent_id — background subagent spans nest under the dispatching Agent tool span for correct trace hierarchy claude_code.tool_result Tool finishes executing tool_name, success, duration_ms, tool_use_id, tool_input_size_bytes claude_code.api_request API call to Claude completes model, cost_usd, input/output tokens claude_code.api_error API call fails (after retries) error, status_code, attempt count claude_code.tool_decision Tool permission accept/reject tool_name, decision, source, tool_use_id claude_code.skill_activated Skill is invoked skill_name, invocation_trigger ( user-slash | claude-proactive | nested-skill ) claude_code.at_mention @-mention is resolved mention_target, resolution_result Opt-in Detail Levels OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 includes prompt text. OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 adds tool parameters (bash commands, MCP names, file paths). OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1 includes the model's response text (v2.1.193). All three are redacted by default for privacy. Enterprise Configuration ▼ Admins can push OTel settings to all users via managed settings (MDM-distributed) so individual developers don't need to configure anything. // Managed settings file — distributed via MDM { "env" : { "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY" : "1" , "OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER" : "otlp" , "OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER" : "otlp" , "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT" : "http://collector.example.com:4317" } } Multi-team segmentation — use OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES="department=eng,team.id=platform,cost_center=123" to tag metrics by team. As of v2.1.161, these values are included as labels on every metric datapoint — slice by team or repo in Grafana/Datadog without a secondary join Dynamic auth — set "otelHeadersHelper": "/path/to/script.sh" in settings.json to auto-refresh tokens (runs every 29 min); as of v2.1.193, the helper also re-runs and reconnects automatically when a tool call returns 401 or 403 — token expiry no longer requires a session restart Cardinality control — toggle OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID , OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_VERSION , and OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ACCOUNT_UUID to tune storage vs. granularity Survey re-opt-in — set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY_FOR_OTEL=1 to re-enable the session quality survey for enterprises capturing responses through OpenTelemetry (the survey is suppressed by default when OTEL is active to avoid polluting telemetry pipelines) Distributed Traces (Beta) ▼ Link every user prompt to the API requests and tool executions it triggers as a single distributed trace. Requires both telemetry flags: export CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 export CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1 export OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=otlp Bash subprocesses inherit a TRACEPARENT env var for W3C trace context propagation — but OTEL_* configuration vars (exporter, endpoint, headers) are intentionally not inherited, so OTEL-instrumented apps run via the Bash tool use their own OTEL config and won't accidentally pick up the CLI's OTLP endpoint Span content redacted by default — set OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 to include tool I/O (truncated at 60 KB) Visualize in Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo, or any OTel-compatible backend Recommended Backends ▼ Signal Options Metrics Prometheus, ClickHouse, Datadog, Honeycomb Logs / Events Elasticsearch, Loki, ClickHouse, Datadog Traces Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb For DAU/WAU/MAU metrics, choose a backend that supports efficient unique-value queries (e.g., ClickHouse, Honeycomb). Privacy & Security ▼ Opt-in only — telemetry requires explicit CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 No code content — raw file contents and code snippets are never included in metrics or events Prompts redacted — only prompt length is recorded unless OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 is set Responses redacted — assistant response text excluded unless OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1 is set; when unset, follows OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS — set OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=0 explicitly to keep prompts-only logging (v2.1.193) Tool inputs redacted — tool parameters excluded unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 is set Trace content redacted — span I/O excluded unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 (truncated at 60 KB) Email included with OAuth — user.email is sent when authenticated via OAuth; configure your backend to filter if needed ROI Measurement Guide Anthropic provides a ready-to-use monitoring starter kit with Docker Compose configs, Prometheus + OTel setup, and Linear integration templates for automated productivity reports. github.com/anthropics/claude-code-monitoring-guide

text: Enterprise Configuration ▼ Admins can push OTel settings to all users via managed settings (MDM-distributed) so individual developers don't need to configure anything. // Managed settings file — distributed via MDM { "env" : { "CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY" : "1" , "OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER" : "otlp" , "OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER" : "otlp" , "OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT" : "http://collector.example.com:4317" } } Multi-team segmentation — use OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES="department=eng,team.id=platform,cost_center=123" to tag metrics by team. As of v2.1.161, these values are included as labels on every metric datapoint — slice by team or repo in Grafana/Datadog without a secondary join Dynamic auth — set "otelHeadersHelper": "/path/to/script.sh" in settings.json to auto-refresh tokens (runs every 29 min); as of v2.1.193, the helper also re-runs and reconnects automatically when a tool call returns 401 or 403 — token expiry no longer requires a session restart Cardinality control — toggle OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID , OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_VERSION , and OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ACCOUNT_UUID to tune storage vs. granularity Survey re-opt-in — set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY_FOR_OTEL=1 to re-enable the session quality survey for enterprises capturing responses through OpenTelemetry (the survey is suppressed by default when OTEL is active to avoid polluting telemetry pipelines)

title: Closing the Loop: From Incident to Intent
label: 17 — Production Monitoring & Control Bands
text: 17 — Production Monitoring & Control Bands Closing the Loop: From Incident to Intent The FSAD workflow (intent → spec → plan → execution → review) is a forward pipeline. A production breach should re-enter that same pipeline automatically, not wait for a human to file a ticket. This is the "Maintain" stage: a monitoring agent watches a rolling-baseline production metric and escalates through statistical control bands. Control Bands: 1σ / 2σ / 3σ ▼ Pick a rolling-baseline metric that reflects delivery or system health — CI test failure rate, post-deploy 5xx rate, or PR cycle time all work. Compute a rolling mean and standard deviation over a trailing window, then respond to breaches in tiers instead of a single fixed threshold: Tier Trigger Response 1σ Metric drifts one standard deviation from baseline Log only — no agent action, just a recorded data point 2σ Metric crosses two standard deviations Claude runs a read-only diagnosis — inspects logs, recent deploys, and traces to form a hypothesis, no changes made 3σ Metric crosses three standard deviations Claude proposes a fix — opens a PR, or executes a pre-approved runbook, gated by the same human-review checkpoint as any other change A rolling baseline (not a fixed threshold) matters because it adapts to normal seasonal or growth-driven drift — you're watching for anomalies relative to recent behavior, not an arbitrary static number that goes stale. Closing the Loop: Breach → Intent ▼ The output of a 2σ or 3σ diagnosis is not a Slack message — it's a new intent.md -style markdown artifact, written in the same format Phase 1 of the workflow produces. That artifact captures what broke, the suspected cause, and supporting evidence (logs, traces, the suspect deploy), then hands off to a human for triage exactly like any other intent. This is what makes the loop closed rather than linear: a production incident doesn't require a human to notice, reproduce, and write up the problem before planning can start. The agent has already done that framing work by the time a human looks at it — the incident re-enters the pipeline at Phase 1 (Intent & Discovery) as a pre-drafted problem statement, then flows through spec, plan, execution, and review like any other change. # bands.yaml — control-band config for a monitoring agent metric: post_deploy_5xx_rate baseline_window: 14d bands: - sigma: 1 action: log - sigma: 2 action: diagnose # read-only: Claude inspects logs/traces, no changes output: intent.md # drafted, not filed — awaits human triage - sigma: 3 action: propose_fix # Claude opens a PR or runs a pre-approved runbook require_human_review: true This Is Phase 1 of the Workflow, Not a New Pipeline The breach-generated intent.md is deliberately shaped like any other Workflow Phase 1 artifact. No separate incident-response track exists — production monitoring feeds the same intent → spec → plan → execution → review loop, so "Maintain" is the phase that turns the pipeline into a closed loop instead of a one-way street.

title: Codex CLI Best Practices
label: 01 — Getting Started
text: 01 — Getting Started Codex CLI Best Practices From installation to agentic workflows with OpenAI's Codex. Codex CLI is OpenAI's open-source coding agent — a terminal UI (TUI) that reads files, writes code, and runs shell commands in a sandbox. It defaults to gpt-5.5 and supports multiple model providers including OpenAI, Azure, Ollama, Bedrock, and more. If your team uses OpenAI models or wants multi-provider flexibility, Codex is the FSAD-compatible agent to learn. Tool-Agnostic by Design FSAD is a methodology, not a tool. While this playbook focuses on Claude Code, the same principles — spec-driven development, markdown layer, agentic workflows — apply to Codex, Gemini CLI, and other coding agents. This section helps teams that use Codex either as their primary tool or alongside Claude Code. Claude Code vs. Codex CLI Concept Claude Code Codex CLI Project instructions CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md Config directory ~/.claude/ ~/.codex/ Config format settings.json (JSON) config.toml (TOML) Default model Claude Sonnet / Opus gpt-5.5 / codex-mini Approval modes Default, Plan, Bypass Auto, Read-only, Full Access Sandbox Per-tool permissions read-only / workspace-write / full-access MCP support Client Client + Server IDE extensions VS Code VS Code, Cursor, Devin Desktop Skills directory .claude/skills/ .agents/skills/ Multi-agent Subagents (Task tool) Agent threads ( max_threads config) Hooks 27 event types (SessionStart, PreToolUse, MessageDisplay, Stop…) 9 event types (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, Stop, Interrupt, PreCompact, PostCompact) Plugin marketplace claude plugin install codex plugin install / /plugins TUI Permission model Per-tool allow/deny + 5 approval modes Named permission profiles with filesystem + network policies Getting Started with Codex 1 Install Codex Install globally via npm or Homebrew: # npm npm install -g @openai/codex # Homebrew (macOS) brew install --cask codex 2 Authenticate Codex supports two authentication methods. On first run it will prompt you to log in with your ChatGPT account, or you can set an API key: # Option A: ChatGPT account (prompted on first run) codex # Option B: API key export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... 3 Create AGENTS.md This is Codex's equivalent of CLAUDE.md — your project instructions file at the repo root: # AGENTS.md ## Project Overview E-commerce platform built with Next.js 14, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. ## Tech Stack - Frontend: Next.js 14, React, Tailwind CSS - Backend: tRPC, Drizzle ORM - Database: PostgreSQL 16 - Testing: Vitest, Playwright ## Conventions - Use server components by default - All database queries go through Drizzle ORM - Run `pnpm test` before committing - Follow existing patterns in src/ 4 First Run Start Codex with a simple task to verify everything works: # Interactive TUI codex # Or start with a prompt codex "describe this project and suggest improvements" AGENTS.md: Project Instructions ▼ Codex merges instructions from multiple AGENTS.md files in a top-down hierarchy. Later files override earlier ones: # Priority order (highest → lowest): 1. ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md # Global overrides (highest priority) 2. ~/.codex/AGENTS.md # Global defaults 3. <repo-root>/AGENTS.md # Project-level instructions 4. <cwd>/AGENTS.md # Sub-directory specifics Key differences from CLAUDE.md : Override files — AGENTS.override.md takes highest priority, useful for personal preferences that override team defaults Size limit — 32 KiB by default (configurable via project_doc_max_bytes in config.toml ) Disable flag — Skip with --no-project-doc or CODEX_DISABLE_PROJECT_DOC=1 Dual-Tool Teams If your team uses both Claude Code and Codex, maintain both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in the same repo. Keep shared conventions (tech stack, testing rules, coding standards) consistent across both files. Running Both Tools Many FSAD teams use both Claude Code and Codex. Keep a CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md in your repo with shared conventions. Use each tool's strengths: Claude Code for Anthropic model quality, Codex for OpenAI model access and multi-provider flexibility. The FSAD workflow — spec → plan → implement → review — works identically regardless of which agent executes.

title: Codex Needs 4 Things
label: 02 — Project Anatomy
text: 02 — Project Anatomy Codex Needs 4 Things The instructions, the skills, the guardrails, the context. Same principles as Claude — different file names. Key Insight Prompting is temporary. Structure is permanent. A well-organized project gives Codex context automatically — every session, every agent thread, every teammate. Pillar 1: AGENTS.md = Repo Memory ▼ Contains WHY (purpose), WHAT (repo map), HOW (rules + commands). Codex reads this file automatically at the start of every session. The 4-level hierarchy lets you layer global defaults with project-specific overrides. # AGENTS.md ## Project Overview E-commerce API — Node.js + PostgreSQL . Handles product catalog, orders, and payments. ## Tech Stack - Runtime: Node.js 20 , TypeScript - Database: PostgreSQL 15 + Prisma ORM - Testing: Vitest , coverage > 80% ## Commands - `npm run dev` — start dev server - `npm test` — run tests - `npm run lint` — lint + format ## Rules - Never modify migration files after they've been applied - All API endpoints require authentication middleware - Use Zod for request validation, not manual checks Tip Codex merges AGENTS.md from 4 levels: ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md (highest) → ~/.codex/AGENTS.md → repo root → current directory. Max 32 KiB by default. The repo-root and sub-directory levels only load in trusted projects — as of rust-v0.150.0, an untrusted project supplies no project-level AGENTS.md instructions. For hooks and tool policies, the equivalent cascade runs through config.toml — add a requirements.toml at system/org level to enforce constraints users cannot override. Pillar 2: .agents/skills/ = Reusable Expert Modes ▼ Turn common workflows into skills. Codex skills live in .agents/skills/ and use a SKILL.md file. Each skill can include scripts, references, and assets alongside the markdown. # .agents/skills/code-review/SKILL.md # Code Review ## Process 1. Check for security vulnerabilities (OWASP Top 10) 2. Verify error handling covers edge cases 3. Check test coverage for new code paths 4. Review naming conventions match project style 5. Verify no secrets or credentials in code ## Checklist - [ ] No SQL injection vectors - [ ] Input validation on all endpoints - [ ] Tests cover happy path + error cases - [ ] No console.log statements left behind Pillar 3: .rules Files = Guardrails ▼ Codex uses the Shell Tool MCP with .rules files for deterministic guardrails — allowing, prompting, or forbidding specific shell commands. Models forget. Rules don't. # .rules — Shell command policies allow npm test allow npm run lint allow npm run build prompt npm install * # Ask before installing packages forbid rm -rf * # Never allow recursive delete forbid git push --force # Never allow force push Important Rules intercept execve(2) calls, so they know the full path of executed programs. This is more granular than Claude's hooks — you control command execution at the shell level. Pillar 4: docs/ = Progressive Context ▼ Architecture overview, ADRs, runbooks. Don't bloat AGENTS.md — put detailed docs in files Codex can read when needed. Same pattern as Claude. docs/ ├── architecture.md # System design overview ├── adr/ # Architecture Decision Records │ ├── 001-use-prisma.md │ ├── 002-auth-strategy.md │ └── 003-caching-layer.md ├── runbooks/ # Operational procedures │ ├── deploy.md │ └── incident-response.md └── api/ # API documentation └── endpoints.md Codex discovers and reads these files on demand when working in related areas. The key is progressive context — only loaded when relevant. Pillar 5: Local AGENTS.md for Risky Modules ▼ Place small AGENTS.md files near sharp edges. Codex sees gotchas exactly when working in that directory. # src/auth/AGENTS.md ## Critical: Authentication Module - NEVER modify the JWT signing key rotation logic - Token refresh uses sliding window — do not change to fixed expiry - Rate limiting is per-IP, configured in middleware (not here) - All changes to this module require security review - Test with: `npm test -- --grep "auth"` Good candidates: src/auth/ , src/billing/ , src/persistence/ , infra/ Project Structure Map my-project/ ├── AGENTS.md # Repo memory (auto-loaded) ├── .codex/ │ └── config.toml # Project settings ├── .agents/ │ └── skills/ # Reusable expert modes │ ├── code-review/ │ │ └── SKILL.md │ └── deploy/ │ ├── SKILL.md │ └── scripts/ │ └── check-staging.sh ├── .rules # Shell command guardrails ├── docs/ # Progressive context │ ├── architecture.md │ └── adr/ ├── src/ │ ├── auth/ │ │ └── AGENTS.md # Local guardrails │ └── billing/ │ └── AGENTS.md # Local guardrails └── spec.md # Feature specification

title: Connect Codex to Your Tools via MCP
label: 03 — Integrations
text: 03 — Integrations Connect Codex to Your Tools via MCP Add MCP servers with the codex mcp add command or edit config.toml directly. Codex CLI ──▶ MCP Protocol ──▶ JIRA ──▶ Figma ──▶ Notion ──▶ Azure DevOps ──▶ Google Workspace Setting Up MCP Connections via codex mcp Codex uses the codex mcp CLI to manage MCP servers. For HTTP servers (Jira, Figma, Notion), use --url . For stdio servers (Azure DevOps, community tools), pass the command after -- . Tool search by default (rust-v0.142.2): Codex now uses MCP tool search by default when the selected model supports it — tools are discovered on demand rather than loaded all at once at session start. This speeds up startup with large MCP server inventories and improves tool discovery. If you need a server's tools always available without deferral, add "alwaysLoad": true to that server's entry in ~/.codex/config.toml . Interactive MCP tool authentication (rust-v0.144.0): MCP tools can now request user authentication mid-session without any experimental opt-in flag — interactive auth flows (OAuth prompts, credential dialogs) are fully supported out of the box. MCP 2026-07-28 protocol support (rust-v0.147.0, opt-in): adds paginated tool discovery for large server inventories, multi-round requests, and non-blocking server startup — Codex no longer waits on a slow-starting MCP server before the session becomes usable. OAuth reauthentication recovery (rust-v0.148.0): MCP servers now recover after OAuth reauthentication without restarting Codex — re-run codex mcp login <name> mid-session and the server reconnects in place. Reauthentication failures report clearer errors about which server needs attention, servers can pin their own OAuth callback port, and dynamic HTTP header helpers are supported for servers that need per-request headers. 1 Add an MCP Server Use codex mcp add to register a server. For hosted HTTP endpoints, use --url : # HTTP server (hosted endpoint) codex mcp add atlassian --url https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp # Stdio server (local process) codex mcp add ado -- npx -y @azure-devops/mcp your-org-name # Stdio server with env vars codex mcp add my-server --env API_KEY=xxx -- npx -y @some/mcp-server 2 Authenticate via OAuth For servers that support OAuth, run codex mcp login . A browser window opens for authentication: codex mcp login atlassian 3 Verify the Connection Use /mcp inside the Codex TUI or codex mcp list from the terminal to confirm servers are connected: # In the Codex TUI: /mcp # From the terminal: codex mcp list 4 Manage Servers Use codex mcp subcommands to manage your connections: codex mcp list # List all configured servers codex mcp get <name> # Show server details codex mcp remove <name> # Remove a server codex mcp login <name> # OAuth login for a server codex mcp logout <name> # Clear OAuth credentials CLI vs. Config File Use codex mcp add for quick setup — it writes to ~/.codex/config.toml automatically. Edit config.toml directly when you need advanced options like startup_timeout_sec , enabled_tools allowlists, or project-scoped servers ( .codex/config.toml in trusted projects). Available Integrations JIRA MCP ▼ What it does: Read, create, and update JIRA issues directly from Codex. Search issues, transition statuses, add comments, and manage sprints. # Add via CLI codex mcp add atlassian --url https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp codex mcp login atlassian # Or in ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.atlassian] url = "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp" Figma MCP ▼ What it does: Read Figma designs, extract component specs, colors, typography, and layout details. # Add via CLI codex mcp add figma --url https://mcp.figma.com/mcp codex mcp login figma # Or in ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.figma] url = "https://mcp.figma.com/mcp" Notion MCP ▼ What it does: Search, read, create, and update Notion pages and databases. # Add via CLI codex mcp add notion --url https://mcp.notion.com/mcp codex mcp login notion # Or in ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.notion] url = "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp" Azure DevOps MCP ▼ What it does: Manage work items, repos, pipelines, wikis, test plans, and advanced security. Microsoft's official MCP server with browser-based OAuth. # Add via CLI (stdio server) codex mcp add ado -- npx -y @azure-devops/mcp your-org-name # Or in ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.ado] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "@azure-devops/mcp", "your-org-name"] Requires Node.js 20+. Browser-based OAuth on first use. See microsoft/azure-devops-mcp . Google Workspace MCP ▼ What it does: Google offers hosted MCP servers for Cloud infrastructure (BigQuery, Cloud SQL, GKE, etc.). Workspace products (Docs, Sheets, Drive) are not yet available as hosted endpoints — use a community server for those. Google Cloud MCP (official, hosted) # Add via CLI — example: BigQuery codex mcp add bigquery --url https://bigquery.googleapis.com/mcp # Or in ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.bigquery] url = "https://bigquery.googleapis.com/mcp" Requires gcloud auth application-default login and gcloud beta services mcp enable SERVICE . See Google Cloud MCP docs . Google Workspace MCP (community, self-hosted) # Add via CLI (build from source first) codex mcp add google-workspace -- /path/to/google_workspace_mcp Requires building from source (Rust) and a Google Cloud project with OAuth. See taylorwilsdon/google_workspace_mcp . Codex as MCP Server Unlike Claude Code, Codex can act as a tool other agents invoke. As of 2026-08-24, the codex mcp-server command is deprecated — use the Codex app server instead for programmatic integration. To use Codex from within Claude Code specifically, use the Codex plugin for Claude Code . Full MCP docs at developers.openai.com/codex/mcp . Codex Chrome Extension OpenAI released a Codex Chrome extension (May 2026) that gives Codex direct browser access — a different integration model from MCP. Instead of routing through an API, Codex reads and acts on the current browser context. Capability Details Parallel tab operation Runs across multiple tabs simultaneously without taking over the browser Per-site access control Users grant Codex access on a site-by-site basis — not all-or-nothing Browser context injection Codex can read page content, fill forms, and interact with web-based tools (Jira, Figma, Notion, Linear) without an MCP server Chrome Extension vs. MCP Use the Chrome extension for web-based tools where you need direct page interaction (reading tickets, filling fields, navigating UI). Use MCP for tools with stable APIs — MCP is more reliable for structured data and automated pipelines. Both can be active simultaneously.

title: Built-in Code Review with /review
label: 04 — Code Review
text: 04 — Code Review Built-in Code Review with /review Codex includes a native code review command that analyzes diffs without modifying your code. How /review Works The /review slash command analyzes your current diff (staged and unstaged changes) and provides feedback on bugs, security issues, code quality, and style — without making any modifications to your files. Usage 1 Start a Codex Session Launch Codex in your project directory: codex 2 Run /review Type /review to analyze your current changes. Codex examines the diff and provides structured feedback: # Review current working tree changes /review # Or ask for a specific review focus "Review the changes in src/auth/ for security issues" 3 Act on Feedback Review the findings and ask Codex to fix specific issues, or continue working on your own. Review Isn't Only Manual (rust-v0.148.0) /review is no longer the only path into review. Automatic review is enforced for managed models — under a managed configuration, review runs on its own rather than waiting for you to invoke it. Strict automatic review is also enforced for MCP tool calls , so tool invocations routed through MCP servers are reviewed before they proceed. Expect review to fire without being asked in enterprise and managed deployments. Claude Code Comparison Claude Code uses a multi-agent fleet for code review (multiple specialized agents in parallel). Codex's /review is single-agent by default but can leverage multi-agent threads if configured. Both approaches catch bugs — Claude's is more comprehensive, Codex's is faster for quick reviews.

title: Turn Repeatable Workflows into Reusable Expert Modes
label: 05 — Building Skills
text: 05 — Building Skills Turn Repeatable Workflows into Reusable Expert Modes Codex skills are markdown-driven workflows stored in .agents/skills/ — each skill gets its own directory with a SKILL.md file. What are Codex Skills? Skills are markdown instructions that Codex follows when invoked. Unlike Claude's flat .claude/skills/ files, Codex skills use a directory structure: each skill has a folder containing SKILL.md plus optional scripts, references, and asset files. Skill Directory Structure .agents/skills/ ├── code-review/ │ └── SKILL.md # Skill instructions ├── deploy/ │ ├── SKILL.md # Skill instructions │ ├── scripts/ │ │ └── check-staging.sh # Helper scripts │ └── references/ │ └── deploy-checklist.md └── estimate/ └── SKILL.md Example: Deployment Skill Deploy Skill — SKILL.md ▼ --- name : deploy description : Guided deployment to staging and production with smoke-test gates model : gpt-5.5 --- # Deployment Skill ## Overview Guided deployment to staging and production environments. ## Process 1. Run the test suite: `npm test` 2. Check for uncommitted changes: `git status` 3. Run the staging check script: `./scripts/check-staging.sh` 4. Build the production bundle: `npm run build` 5. Deploy to staging: `npm run deploy:staging` 6. Run smoke tests against staging 7. If smoke tests pass, deploy to production ## Safety Rules - NEVER deploy directly to production without staging - Always check the deploy-checklist.md reference - Abort if any test or smoke test fails Skill Frontmatter & Validation (rust-v0.148.0) Codex parses model annotations in skill frontmatter — add model: to pin which model a skill runs on. Skill validation also rejects unfinished TODO placeholders , so a scaffolded SKILL.md must be filled in before it will load. The bundled skill-creator guide was tightened to match. Best Practice Start with one skill for your most repeated workflow. Codex skills can include shell scripts and reference docs alongside the markdown — use this for deployment checklists, migration procedures, or incident response runbooks.

title: Lessons from Real-World Codex Adoption
label: 06 — Guidelines
text: 06 — Guidelines Lessons from Real-World Codex Adoption Practical guidance for teams using Codex for spec-driven agentic development. Prompting Be Specific About What, Not How Tell Codex what outcome you want, not the implementation steps. Let the agent choose the approach based on codebase context. Provide Business Context Include business requirements, constraints, and existing patterns. "We need a user preferences API because mobile users complain about notification noise" is better than "add a PATCH endpoint." Use Tab for File References Press Tab to fuzzy-search files by name (prefix with @ ). This ensures the right context is loaded and prevents Codex from searching in the wrong places. Use /plan Mode First For complex features, start with /plan . Let Codex analyze and propose before making changes. Review the plan, then let it execute. Project Structure Keep AGENTS.md Focused Stay under the 32 KiB limit. Put detailed docs in docs/ for progressive context — don't bloat your project instructions file. Use Skills for Repeatable Workflows If you find yourself giving the same instructions across sessions, encode them as a skill in .agents/skills/ . Use Local AGENTS.md for Sensitive Modules Place small AGENTS.md files near auth, billing, and infrastructure code. Codex sees the guardrails exactly when working in that directory. Use /compact to Manage Context Long conversations eat context. Use /compact to summarize the conversation and free up tokens for the agent to work with. Anti-Patterns to Avoid Over-Permissive Sandbox Using danger-full-access outside of containers defeats the security model. Stick with workspace-write for development. Bloated AGENTS.md Stuffing every rule into AGENTS.md defeats the purpose. Keep it focused on high-level rules; use docs/ and local AGENTS.md for details. Ignoring Session Resume Codex saves sessions automatically. Use codex resume to pick up where you left off instead of re-explaining context from scratch. Not Using /compact Long conversations degrade agent performance. Use /compact regularly to summarize and free context tokens. Project Trust & Managed Auth As of rust-v0.147.0, Codex requires explicit trust before running in an unfamiliar local project — you'll be prompted to confirm the first time Codex operates in a new directory, similar to how project-scoped MCP servers and hooks already only load in trusted projects. Managed authentication restrictions are also enforced before credentials are used, not after, closing a window where an untrusted project could exercise credentials prior to the trust check completing. As of rust-v0.150.0, untrusted projects no longer supply project-level AGENTS.md instructions at all — until you trust the directory, only your global ~/.codex/AGENTS.md layers apply, closing a prompt-injection path from unfamiliar repos. Security Review The sec-review-team skill is model-agnostic — it spawns Claude Code agents internally to run a multi-specialist security review, but its output (REPORT.md + FINDINGS.jsonl) is a workflow any team can adopt regardless of which CLI they use day-to-day. Codex teams can run the review via Claude Code and apply the fixes directly in their Codex workflow.

title: Hooks — Automation & Guardrails
label: 07 — Hooks
text: 07 — Hooks Hooks — Automation & Guardrails Event-driven shell commands that fire deterministically at specific points in the agent loop. Models forget. Hooks don't. Hooks inject scripts into Codex's agentic loop at named lifecycle events. Unlike instructions in AGENTS.md that the model may or may not follow, hooks always execute when their event triggers — making them ideal for audit logging, policy enforcement, and automated validation. Generally Available — May 2026 Codex Hooks reached General Availability on 2026-05-14. They are production-ready with no feature flag required — [features] codex_hooks = true is the default and stable for use in production pipelines, enterprise environments, and automated workflows. Hook Event Types Event When it fires Can block? Claude Code equivalent SessionStart Session begins or resumes No — adds context only SessionStart UserPromptSubmit User submits a prompt Yes (exit 2) UserPromptSubmit PreToolUse Before Bash, apply_patch , or MCP tool runs; hooks can inject additional context into the turn by returning a context field in JSON output Yes (exit 2 or deny JSON) PreToolUse PermissionRequest When Codex seeks approval (shell escalation, network) Yes — allow / deny PermissionRequest PostToolUse After tool completes (including failed runs) Yes (exit 2 — replaces output) PostToolUse Stop When a turn completes Yes — can request continuation Stop Interrupt When an active top-level turn is interrupted (e.g. you cancel mid-turn); can run commands or MCP handlers (rust-v0.150.0) No — the turn is already stopping — (no direct equivalent) PreCompact Before context compaction runs Yes (exit 2 blocks compaction) PreCompact PostCompact After context compaction completes No PostCompact Configuration Enable hooks with [features] codex_hooks = true (default). Define hooks inline in config.toml or in a separate hooks.json . Project-scoped hooks go in .codex/config.toml and only load in trusted projects. Async and MCP-tool hooks (rust-v0.148.0): a hook can now run asynchronously — Codex fires it and continues the turn instead of waiting for it to finish — and a hook can invoke an MCP tool directly instead of shelling out to a script. Hook listings show each hook's execution mode, so blocking hooks are distinguishable from background ones at a glance. A hook that exceeds its timeout now has its entire process tree terminated rather than just the top-level process, so orphaned children no longer linger, and hook runtimes refresh after plugin changes. config.toml hook syntax ▼ # ~/.codex/config.toml (global) or .codex/config.toml (project) [features] codex_hooks = true # Fire before every Bash call [[hooks.PreToolUse]] matcher = "^Bash$" [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]] type = "command" command = "/usr/bin/python3 ~/.codex/hooks/check-command.py" timeout = 10 statusMessage = "Checking command safety" # Fire after any apply_patch / Edit / Write [[hooks.PostToolUse]] matcher = "apply_patch" [[hooks.PostToolUse.hooks]] type = "command" command = "/usr/bin/python3 ~/.codex/hooks/audit-log.py" Exit Code Semantics Exit code Meaning 0 + valid JSON Process output per event schema (allow, deny, inject context, request continuation) 0 + plain text Append as developer context (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit) 0 + no output Pass-through — hook ran successfully, no action taken 2 Block / deny; read reason from stderr; exact behavior depends on event type Recipes Recipe: Block dangerous shell commands (PreToolUse) ▼ #!/usr/bin/env python3 import json, sys, re hook_input = json.load(sys.stdin) command = hook_input[ "tool_input" ].get( "command" , "" ) if re.search( r"rm\s+-rf|sudo\s+rm|DROP\s+TABLE" , command): print(json.dumps({ "hookSpecificOutput" : { "hookEventName" : "PreToolUse" , "permissionDecision" : "deny" , "permissionDecisionReason" : "High-risk command blocked by policy" } })) sys.exit(0) Recipe: Detect API keys in prompts (UserPromptSubmit) ▼ #!/usr/bin/env python3 import json, sys, re hook_input = json.load(sys.stdin) prompt = hook_input.get( "prompt" , "" ) if re.search( r"sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{20,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}" , prompt): sys.stderr.write( "Possible API key or AWS credential detected in prompt\n" ) sys.exit(2) # blocks the prompt submission Recipe: Audit-log every tool call (PostToolUse) ▼ #!/usr/bin/env python3 import json, sys, datetime, pathlib hook_input = json.load(sys.stdin) log_entry = { "ts" : datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(), "session" : hook_input[ "session_id" ], "tool" : hook_input[ "tool_name" ], "input" : hook_input[ "tool_input" ], } log_path = pathlib.Path.home() / ".codex" / "audit.jsonl" with log_path.open( "a" ) as f: f.write(json.dumps(log_entry) + "\n" ) # Exit 0 with no output = pass-through Claude Code Comparison Codex has 9 hook event types; Claude Code has more (26 total events including SubagentStart, TaskCreated, FileChanged, PreCompact, etc.). Both use the same input-via-stdin / exit-code pattern. If you're migrating hook scripts, the core logic is portable — only the event names and JSON shape differ slightly.
