title: Everything You Need in One Place
label: 08 — Codex Cheat Sheet
text: 08 — Codex Cheat Sheet Everything You Need in One Place Keyboard shortcuts, commands, flags, configuration, and environment variables. Keyboard Shortcuts Key Action Enter Inject instructions into current turn Ctrl+C Close session / cancel Ctrl+L Clear screen Ctrl+G Open external editor for longer prompts Esc Esc Edit previous user message (keep pressing to walk back) Tab / @ Unified context picker — type @ to search files, directories, plugins, and skills in one picker (backed by app-server plugin metadata). Added in v0.131.0. As of rust-v0.150.0 you can also @ -mention other Codex tasks to reference them in your prompt. ↑ / ↓ Navigate draft history in composer Alt+, Lower reasoning level for current model Alt+. Raise reasoning level for current model Slash Commands Command Action /plan Enter plan mode — propose before implementing /review Analyze diffs without modifying code /goal Create a persisted goal; browse discoverable goals in TUI. Goals pause across session resume by default — opt back in from the picker. Supports multi-day duration tracking. /fork Clone conversation to a new thread, including paginated history from the parent. Choose "temporary" in the picker (or use the --temp flag) for forks that don't appear in thread listings — ideal for exploratory side work (rust-v0.146.0). /side Open an ephemeral branch for a focused follow-up; doesn't pollute main context. Switch between open side conversations without closing them (rust-v0.146.0). /new /clear Start a fresh conversation within the same CLI session (both commands are equivalent). Use the thread picker to pin important threads for quick access, and organize them into persistent, manually ordered sections (rust-v0.146.0, extended rust-v0.147.0). /archive Archive the current session — protected from resume or fork until restored. CLI: codex archive / codex unarchive , or archive and restore directly from the resume picker. (v0.136.0, picker support rust-v0.148.0) /delete Permanently delete the current session with confirmation. Cleans up subagent threads. Also available as codex delete . (v0.140.0) /compact Summarize conversation to free context tokens /diff Show current changes (staged and unstaged); workspace-aware — diff is scoped to your project root /cd <path> Change the session's working directory (rust-v0.149.0) /pwd Print the session's current working directory (rust-v0.149.0) /cwd Print the session's current working directory (rust-v0.149.0) /model Switch model and/or reasoning level mid-session /fast Toggle fast mode ( on / off / status ) /agent Switch between active agent threads /plugins Browse, install, and manage marketplace plugins /apps Browse and insert available connectors /ide Inject IDE file/editor context into the current session (workspace-aware) /mcp List configured MCP tools /permissions Change approval mode mid-session /init Generate an AGENTS.md scaffold for the current project /import Migrate settings, MCP servers, plugins, sessions, commands, and project-scoped memories from Cursor or Claude Code . Selectively import any combination for full cross-tool migration. (v0.140.0, expanded v0.145.0) As of rust-v0.147.0, also imports Cursor-managed skills, and re-running the import synchronizes changes to previously-imported Claude/Cursor conversations without creating duplicates. /vim Toggle Vim modal editing in the composer. Set vim_mode = true in config.toml to enable by default. /keymap [debug] Remap TUI keyboard shortcuts interactively. As of rust-v0.150.0 you can bind shortcuts to cycle through permission modes. Use /keymap debug to inspect raw terminal key events — helpful when Vim mode or chord bindings don't register. /statusline Configure footer status items — including the estimated thread credits/cost item for eligible workspaces (rust-v0.148.0) /hooks Browse and toggle configured hooks from the TUI without editing config files /personality Set agent personality (friendly / pragmatic / none) /copy Copy the latest completed response to clipboard (also Ctrl+O ). As of rust-v0.150.0, opens a picker so you can copy the full response, an individual code block, or a blockquote. /rename Rename the current thread — suggests an editable title based on the conversation. Unnamed terminal tasks also receive descriptive titles automatically. (rust-v0.150.0) /export Export the complete conversation as Markdown — copy it to the clipboard or write it to a new file (rust-v0.148.0) /status Show session config and token usage metrics. For eligible workspaces, also shows estimated thread credits or cost — the same estimate surfaced in status lines and terminal titles (rust-v0.148.0) /usage View daily, weekly, and cumulative account token activity. Redeem earned usage-limit reset credits directly from this view. (v0.140.0) /debug-config Print configuration layers and policy diagnostics /exit Close session CLI Flags Flag Purpose --model / -m Select model (e.g., gpt-5.5 , codex-mini-latest ) --sandbox / -s Set sandbox policy ( read-only , workspace-write , danger-full-access ) --approval-mode / -a Set approval level ( auto , read-only , writes , full-access ). The writes mode allows declared read-only actions automatically while prompting only for write operations (rust-v0.144.0). --approve-for-me Enables automatically reviewed approvals — Codex reviews and approves its own actions against policy instead of prompting you for each one (rust-v0.147.0). --quiet / -q Minimal output for scripting --json JSON Lines output for machine consumption; includes reasoning-token usage -i Attach image / screenshot (multimodal) --full-auto Removed in rust-v0.147.0 — use --sandbox workspace-write instead --profile Apply a named config profile ( ~/.codex/config.toml [profiles.<name>] ) --notify Desktop notifications when tasks complete --no-project-doc Skip AGENTS.md loading --output-schema Enforce JSON Schema on response (use with exec ) --ephemeral No session persistence (use with exec ) codex update Update Codex CLI to the latest version codex remote-control Start a headless, remotely controllable app-server — a simpler entrypoint than configuring the full app-server stack. Allows external clients to drive a Codex session via the protocol API (v0.130.0). Use codex remote-control pair to generate a manual pairing code from a running daemon when automated OAuth pairing isn't available (rust-v0.143.0). codex exec fork Fork an existing session non-interactively from the CLI — branch a thread for scripted or automated follow-up work without opening the TUI (rust-v0.148.0). codex doctor Run support-ready diagnostics across runtime, auth, terminal, network, config, storage, and local state. Added in v0.131.0; storage diagnostics added in rust-v0.148.0. codex agents Open an interactive dashboard to search, start, open, rename, and stop tasks, with configurable shortcuts (rust-v0.149.0). codex queue Send a message to an existing local or remote session without switching into it; reliably wakes idle sessions and resolves duplicate session names (rust-v0.149.0). Configuration Reference Key ( config.toml ) Purpose Default model Default model gpt-5.5 model_reasoning_effort Reasoning depth: minimal / low / medium / high / xhigh medium model_verbosity Response verbosity: low / medium / high medium vim_mode Enable Vim modal editing in the composer by default false approval_policy Approval mode: untrusted / on-request / never / granular on-request sandbox_mode Sandbox policy: read-only / workspace-write / danger-full-access read-only default_permissions Named permission profile to apply by default (e.g. ":workspace" ) — service_tier OpenAI service tier: flex (cheaper) / fast (lower latency) fast web_search Web search mode: disabled / cached / live . Now supported for compatible custom model providers, not just native OpenAI models (rust-v0.146.0). cached project_doc_max_bytes Max AGENTS.md size in bytes 32768 [agents].max_threads Max concurrent agent threads 6 [agents].max_depth Max agent nesting depth 1 [agents].job_max_runtime_seconds Per-worker timeout 3600 [features].codex_hooks Enable the hooks system true [otel] OpenTelemetry export config (exporter, endpoint, metrics) — Environment Variables Variable Purpose OPENAI_API_KEY API key for OpenAI models CODEX_DISABLE_PROJECT_DOC Set to 1 to skip AGENTS.md loading CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE Path to custom CA cert for enterprise proxy / TLS interception SSL_CERT_FILE Alternative CA cert path (covers HTTPS and WebSocket connections) AWS_PROFILE / AWS_REGION AWS credentials for Amazon Bedrock provider. AWS_REGION is optional if ~/.aws/config sets the region (Claude Code v2.1.172 reads it as fallback)

title: Advanced Features for Power Users
label: 09 — Power Usage
text: 09 — Power Usage Advanced Features for Power Users Multi-agent workflows, hooks, plugins, permission profiles, Bedrock, session management, CI/CD, multi-provider models, and Codex Cloud. Multi-Agent Workflows ▼ Codex supports multi-agent threads with configurable concurrency and specialized roles. The V2 multi-agent experience (opt-in) is now stable as of v0.145.0 , with configurable per-agent models and reasoning levels. # ~/.codex/config.toml [agents] max_threads = 6 max_depth = 1 job_max_runtime_seconds = 3600 Per-sub-agent model and reasoning (v0.145.0): Configure different models and reasoning effort levels for each sub-agent role in config.toml : # Per-role model and reasoning overrides [agents.worker] model = "gpt-5.5" reasoning = "medium" [agents.explorer] model = "gpt-5.5" reasoning = "low" Built-in roles: default — Standard agent behavior worker — Focused task execution explorer — Read-only codebase analysis monitor — Long-running observation (up to 1-hour windows) Batch processing: spawn_agents_on_csv reads a CSV and spawns one worker per row — useful for bulk migrations and parallel test generation. Rollout token budgets (v0.142.0): Configure a per-thread token budget to cap token usage across agent threads. When nearing the limit, Codex surfaces remaining-budget reminders; turns abort automatically when the budget is exhausted. Set in config.toml under [agents] : # ~/.codex/config.toml [agents] rollout_token_budget = 100000 # abort turn when budget exceeded rollout_budget_reminder_threshold = 0.8 # warn at 80% consumed Interactive dashboard (rust-v0.149.0): Run codex agents to open an interactive dashboard for day-to-day management of running agent tasks — search, start, open, rename, and stop tasks, with configurable keyboard shortcuts. This is distinct from the [agents] config.toml settings above, which govern concurrency and per-role behavior rather than task management. title: Measuring FSAD Success
label: 01 — FSAD Metrics
text: 01 — FSAD Metrics Measuring FSAD Success What to measure to demonstrate the value of agentic development to your organization. Highest Priority Token Consumption by User Track per-developer AI usage to identify adoption patterns and cost centers. High consumption with high output signals effective use; high consumption with low output signals coaching opportunities. Total Monthly Epics / Tickets Volume of work items completed, comparing pre- vs. post-FSAD adoption. Expect a meaningful increase as AI agents accelerate implementation cycles. Total Monthly Story Points Throughput measurement for sprint-over-sprint comparison. Track velocity trends after FSAD adoption to quantify productivity gains. Total PRs / Commits Development velocity indicator. AI-assisted workflows typically produce higher commit frequency with smaller, more focused changesets. Maintenance vs. New Product Development Breakdown of time and code produced by maintenance vs. new product development. Measures whether AI frees engineering capacity for innovation over sustaining work. Total $ Spend by AI Tool Cost tracking per tool (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) for ROI analysis. Correlate spend against velocity and output metrics to demonstrate return on investment. Other Metrics AI Coding Tools WAU Weekly Active Users across AI coding tools. Measures adoption breadth across the engineering organization. Lines of Code Produced AI-generated vs. human-written code split. Track the ratio over time to understand how AI contribution evolves. AI Commits vs. Acceptance Rates How often AI-generated code is accepted vs. revised. A quality signal — high acceptance rates indicate well-configured agents and effective specs. Start Small Don't instrument everything on day one. Token consumption + story points alone can demonstrate ROI within a single sprint. Add granularity as your FSAD practice matures and leadership asks deeper questions.

title: Process Health Metrics
label: 02 — Process Health
text: 02 — Process Health Process Health Metrics Volume tells you how much work moved. Process health tells you whether it moved safely and fast . Pair a leading (speed) metric with a lagging (quality) metric for each stage of the workflow so a faster cycle time never gets read as progress on its own. Leading Indicators — process speed Spec → Plan Cycle Time Elapsed time from the spec.md commit closing Phase 2 — Live Spec Session to the plan.md commit closing Phase 3 — Implementation Planning . A widening gap usually means the spec left decisions unresolved that the planning agent had to stop and ask about. Plan → Merged PR Cycle Time Elapsed time from plan approval at the end of Phase 3 to a merged PR at the end of Phase 5 — Human Review & Ship , spanning Phase 4 — Parallel Agent Execution . This is the true "idea to production" window agentic development is meant to compress. First-Pass CI Success Rate Share of agent-written changes from Phase 4 — Parallel Agent Execution that pass CI on the first run, with no human-triggered fix-up commit. A reliable proxy for spec clarity and agent-configuration health — low first-pass rates point back to Phase 2 or Phase 3, not to the agent. Lagging Indicators — quality & outcome PR Review Time Human review duration during Phase 5 — Human Review & Ship . If review time climbs while PR size stays flat, treat it as a signal — not noise — that reviewers are compensating for spec drift or agent overreach upstream. Defect / Vulnerability Escape Rate Issues caught during Phase 5 review vs. found post-merge (production incidents, security findings). A rising post-merge share means the review gate isn't catching what agentic velocity now requires it to catch. Repeat-Incident Rate Share of incidents that recur in the same root-cause class within a fixed window (e.g. 90 days) despite a prior fix having shipped. High repeat rates mean the lesson learned isn't making it back into spec.md or plan.md for the next pass through the workflow. Pair, Don't Isolate Never report a cycle-time win without its paired quality metric alongside it. A faster Plan → Merged PR time achieved by cutting corners in Phase 5 review will show up later as a worse defect-escape or repeat-incident rate — track both so speed gains are real, not deferred.

title: Engineer the Economics, Not Just the Adoption
label: 03 — Token Optimization Strategies
text: 03 — Token Optimization Strategies Engineer the Economics, Not Just the Adoption Adoption is no longer the open question — engineering orgs running FSAD at scale have already made agentic development the default. The next problem is system economics: how do you redesign the harness to produce more engineering output from the same, or less, machine intelligence? Three Levers for Token Efficiency Use Less Unnecessary Intelligence Identify where the harness asks models to read, reason, iterate, or coordinate more than the task requires — over-agenting (multiple agents rediscovering the same problem), context that re-teaches the codebase instead of retrieving it progressively, loops that keep iterating past the point of measurable progress, and tickets sized for humans rather than agent-sized work packets. Where are we paying multiple agents to rediscover or reconsider the same problem? Don't Use Intelligence Where Software Will Do Push deterministic work — compiler output, linting, dependency analysis, code search, test execution, schema validation, security scanning — outside the LLM loop. Reduce a 20,000-line build log to "12 failures → 3 root causes → 5 files" before an agent ever sees it. Tools perform computation and filtering; agents perform judgment. What are we currently paying an LLM to read, discover, or calculate that ordinary software could determine deterministically? Buy the Right Intelligence Stop assuming frontier models should do most of the work. Explore a frontier-supervisor architecture — frontier intelligence decomposes and reviews, open-weight models execute bounded implementation — with escalation triggered by repeated failure, low confidence, or security risk rather than static task-type assignment. Should frontier intelligence increasingly become the escalation path rather than the default execution layer? Frontier vs. Open-Weight: Divide the Work Frontier Model Open-Weight Model(s) Frontier Re-engagement Understand the problem Execute bounded implementation tasks Intervene when confidence drops Determine architecture Perform routine refactoring Resolve difficult problems Decompose complex work Generate tests Review architecture Identify risks and constraints Investigate predictable failures Perform high-risk/final validation Define acceptance criteria Execute routine build/test/fix loops Resolve ambiguity and exceptions Open-Weight Isn't Automatically Cheaper The relevant comparison is not cost per million tokens — it's cost per successfully completed engineering task. Inference, infrastructure, retries, latency, engineer intervention, and quality failures all factor in. A weaker model that needs four attempts can end up costlier than a frontier model that succeeds on the first try, which is why hybrid-model experimentation matters more than a blanket cheaper-model switch. Experiments Worth Running Experiment Comparison Agent topology Current multi-agent harness vs. simplified adaptive harness Context architecture Current context strategy vs. progressive retrieval + aggressive compaction Deterministic preprocessing Raw information passed to agent vs. tool-generated structured summaries Convergence Current autonomous loops vs. progress-aware stopping and escalation Task sizing Current ticket structure vs. purpose-built agent work packets Intelligence architecture Frontier-only vs. open-weight-only vs. frontier supervisor + open-weight workers Portfolio Metric to Track Cost per accepted autonomous engineering change. Pair it with the Total $ Spend by AI Tool metric above — spend alone tells you how much you burned; this tells you how much you got for it.
